##### ॥ सायणभाष्यम् ॥ (Sāyaṇa-bhāṣya)

> मरुत्वते । मरुतः स्तोतारः । स्तुतिद्वारेण तद्वते पितृ ऋत्विजां पितृभूताय शिशवे शंसनीयाय हविर्धानशकटयोः सुखासीनभूताय सोमाय सप्त
> च्छंदांसि क्षरंति । स्तुतित्वेन गच्छंति । अपि च पुत्रासोऽपि सोमस्य पुत्रभूता ऋत्विजोऽप्यतं सत्यभूतं स्तोत्रमवीवतन् । संगमयंति । सद्गुणग्राहिणीं स्तुतिं
> कुर्वंतीत्यर्थः । उभे इद्दे एव हविर्धानशकटे अस्योभयस्य देवजातस्य मनुष्यजातस्य च राजतः । ईशाते । उभे एव शकटे यतेते । कर्मानुषा ने प्रयत्नं
> कुरुतः । उभयस्य देवजातस्य मनुष्यजातस्य च पुस्कृतः । हविर्धारणद्यारेण पुष्टिं
> कुरुत इत्यर्थः ॥

##### Gist of the bhāṣya

मरुत्वते (*marutvate*): the Maruts are the praisers; by way of praise, he who has them. To the child, the one to be praised, who is the father of the priests and is seated at ease on the two Havirdhāna carts — to Soma — the seven metres flow, i.e. go as praise. And the sons also, the priests who are sons of Soma, अवीवतन् (*avīvatan*) the true praise, i.e. bring it together; the meaning is that they make praise that seizes good qualities. Both carts rule over both, what is born of the gods and what is born of men. Both carts exert themselves, making effort for the rite. They nourish both, what is born of gods and of men; the meaning is that they bring about nourishment by carrying the oblations.

##### प्रतिपदार्थ (Pratipadārtha)

- मरुत्वते (*marutvate*)—one furnished with praise
- पित्रे (*pitre*)—father to the priests
- शिशवे (*śiśave*)—of the form of a son to the carts; toward Soma
- सप्त (*sapta*)—the seven metres
- क्षरंति (*kṣaraṃti*)—flow in the form of praise
- पुत्रासः अपि (*putrāsaḥ api*)—the priests, sons of Soma
- ऋतं (*ṛtaṃ*)—praise of the nature of truth
- अवीवतन् (*avīvatan*)—offer
- उभे इत् (*ubhe it*)—both these carts
- अस्य उभयस्य (*asya ubhayasya*)—of all, gods, men and others
- राजतः (*rājataḥ*)—are lords
- उभे (*ubhe*)—both these carts
- यतेते (*yatete*)—exert themselves for the rite
- उभयस्य (*ubhayasya*)—for all, gods, men and others
- पुष्यतः (*puṣyataḥ*)—you are nourishers

##### भावार्थ (Bhāvārtha)

Toward Soma, who is furnished with praise, father to the priests and of the form of a son to the carts, the seven metres flow in the form of praise. The priests, sons of Soma, offer praise of the nature of truth.

### Printed p. 428
Both these carts are lords of all, gods, men and others. Both these carts exert themselves for the rite. O carts, you are nourishers of all, gods, men and others.

##### English translation
The seven (metres) offer laudation to the glorious, the adorable parent (the Soma), his sons (the priests) utter his true (praise); you both are lords of both (men and gods), you both exert yourselves and are the nourishers of both (men and gods¹.

## Sūkta 14 (Maṇḍala 10)
In this sūkta and in some following sūktas there are descriptions explaining the Pitṛs, the divisions and subdivisions among them, and the regions or worlds where they dwell. First one must understand what is meant by Pitṛs, who they are and what their nature is. After men who live on earth have died, their earthly body is dissolved and its various parts merge into the five elements, earth and the rest. The five elements are earth, water, air, fire and space. That is, the solid substances in the body, such as bones, merge in time into the earth; the liquid ones, such as blood, into water; the vital airs into air; the fire in the body in the form of heat into fire; and the remainder into space. But there is a vital power that does not dissolve into these five elements. By it all the functions of the body go on while a person lives. It does not perish with the body. Remaining in a subtle form, it stays for a long time experiencing pleasure, pain and the like in the subtle worlds such as heaven, according to the fruit of the deeds it has done. This vital power the Ṛgveda describes by the words ātman, jīva, manas and jyotis. After this ātman is separated from the dead body, it stays for some time in the preta-body and afterwards goes to heaven and the like. It is customary to call the souls of the dead who are in heaven and the like Pitṛs. That is, persons in subtle form, who were our elders, who lived on this earth in the past, before we were born, and who after death still enjoy happiness and delight in the good worlds such as heaven, are called Pitṛs.

### Printed p. 429


Pitṛs, Pitṛlokas and the worship of the Pitṛs.

As the fruit of performing good rites such as sacrifices, a man obtains the status of a pitṛ after death. He is then carried by Yama, the king, to the world that corresponds to his rite. The sentences of the Vedic Saṃhitā praise the pitṛs and Yama in this way:

परेयिवांसं प्रवतो महीरनु बहुभ्यः पंथामनुपस्पशानं । वैवस्वतं संगमनं जनानां यमं राजानं हविषा दुवस्य ॥ (*pareyivāṃsaṃ pravato mahīranu bahubhyaḥ paṃthāmanupaspaśānaṃ | vaivasvataṃ saṃgamanaṃ janānāṃ yamaṃ rājānaṃ haviṣā duvasya ‖*) (Ṛ. Saṃ. 10-14-1)

There are many such mantras. They say: "Worship Yama, the lord who leads good people, who performed excellent rites, to the worlds that grant enjoyments corresponding to each one's rites." Such mantras convey many points of doctrine. It is stated:
1) After death, when the body has perished, the part that is different from the body and is not perishable goes to and reaches the world fixed for it according to its earthly deeds.
2) Such worlds are three in number and are called the Pitṛlokas.
3) Yama, the king of all the pitṛs, is the lord of all these worlds, and the best of them is exceedingly radiant.
4) The pitṛs who dwell in these worlds also, like the gods, bestow their favour on their living sons and others, and accept the oblation in the form of "स्वधा (*svadhā*)" offered by them.

There are many discussions on the question whether the eternal principle that is praised as आत्मा (*ātmā*) in the Upaniṣads and the like, and the power of the self that is described as capable of attaining eternal union (sāyujya), is the same self stated in the Ṛksaṃhitā in the same technical terms, or whether the two descriptions differ. There is no room for that discussion here; its course will be given later, as the context requires and if necessary. In the present context the following matters must necessarily be discussed. When does the qualification to be called a pitṛ arise? For whom? What are their natures? By what kind of rite is the body released after death? How is the part that remains after the body described? What is its final abode? Does the impression of dharma follow after the body? This section may be divided as stated below, and each point examined on the basis of Vedic sentences.

### Printed p. 430
1) The principle (the self) different from the earthly body.
2) The groups of pitṛs and the Pitṛlokas.
3) Rebirth and other births.
4) The rite for the departed (preta).
5) Pitṛ-śrāddha.

1) The principle different from the earthly body and its nature.
The words आत्मन् (*ātman*), अजोभाग (*ajobhāga*), जीव (*jīva*), प्राण (*prāṇa*), मनस् (*manas*), सुवर्ण (*suvarṇa*), असु (*asu*) and ज्योति (*jyoti*) are words denoting the part of the person that is different from the body and not perishable. How this part, which lies beyond the body, is described in the Ṛksaṃhitā and in other Vedic sentences, and how these words reflect that eternal thing, are matters to be examined for now.

The word आत्मन् (*ātman*) is formed from the root आन् (*ān*), which gives meanings such as "to live, to breathe". This word आत्मन् (*ātman*) is used in the Ṛksaṃhitā on many occasions, in altered forms. Usages such as आत्मदाः (*ātmadāḥ*), आत्मवत् (*ātmavat*), आत्मन्वतीभिः (*ātmanvatībhiḥ*), आत्माइव (*ātmāiva*), आत्मनवंतं (*ātmanavaṃtaṃ*), शतात्मा (*śatātmā*) and शतात्मानं (*śatātmānaṃ*) denote the part beyond the body. Its precise meaning cannot be stated as "this, thus". In the commentaries one meaning is given in one place and another elsewhere. For example:

को ददर्श प्रथमं जायमानमस्थन्वंतं यदनस्था बिभर्ति । भूम्या असुरसृगात्मा क्व स्वित्को विद्वांसमुप गात्पष्टुमेतत् ॥ (*ko dadarśa prathamaṃ jāyamānamasthanvaṃtaṃ yadanasthā bibharti | bhūmyā asurasṛgātmā kva svitko vidvāṃsamupa gātpaṣṭumetat ‖*) (Ṛ. Saṃ. 1-164-4)

Here both words असुः (*asuḥ*) and आत्मा (*ātmā*) are used. By भूम्याः असुरसृक् (*bhūmyāḥ asurasṛk*) the earthly gross body is described. Sāyaṇa has explained: असुः प्राणः तदुपलक्षितं सूक्ष्मशरीरं असृक् शोणितं (*asuḥ prāṇaḥ tadupalakṣitaṃ sūkṣmaśarīraṃ asṛk śoṇitaṃ*). Even though the vital breath is of the nature of consciousness, it too is earthly. Within the material body two divisions are made, gross and subtle: the vital breath is classed as the subtle body, and blood and the like as the gross body. Sāyaṇa's explanation also shows that the consciousness in the form of breath differs from the consciousness in the form of the self. When the self is described as पंचभूतात्मक शरीरसंबद्ध चेतनः (*paṃcabhūtātmaka śarīrasaṃbaddha cetanaḥ*), the difference between the material body and the self is shown. The word is also used in the sense of a power that governs the functions of the body. In contexts such as आत्मा ते वातः (*ātmā te vātaḥ*) (7-86-2) it means the power that governs the world. This is beyond the body. Pointing to this very part—

### Printed p. 431
अजो भागस्तपसा तं तपस्व तं ते शोचिस्तपतु तं ते अर्चिः । यास्ते शिवास्तन्वो जातवेदस्ताभिर्वहैनं सुकृतामु लोकं ॥ (*ajo bhāgastapasā taṃ tapasva taṃ te śocistapatu taṃ te arciḥ | yāste śivāstanvo jātavedastābhirvahainaṃ sukṛtāmu lokaṃ ‖*) (Ṛ. Saṃ. 10-16-4)

Here Sāyaṇa, explaining the meaning of the word अज (*aja*), says: अजः जननरहितः शरीरेंद्रियभागव्यतिरिक्तः अंतरपुरुषलक्षणो यो भागोऽस्ति (*ajaḥ jananarahitaḥ śarīreṃdriyabhāgavyatiriktaḥ aṃtarapuruṣalakṣaṇo yo bhāgo 'sti*). It means the part that is without birth, different from the body and the senses, and hidden within the body of the person. In the mantra above, Agni is prayed not to burn this part, not to let it perish, and to make it reach an everlasting place.

The word जीव (*jīva*) is used in the same way. This word is used in many places, but it is not given the same meaning in all contexts. It is used in the sense of a distinct self in two places only:

उदीर्ध्वं जीवो असुर्न आगादप प्रागात्तम आ ज्योतिरेति ॥ (*udīrdhvaṃ jīvo asurna āgādapa prāgāttama ā jyotireti ‖*) (Ṛ. Saṃ. 1-113-16)

जीवो मृतस्य चरति स्वधाभिरमर्त्यो मर्त्येना सयोनिः ॥ (*jīvo mṛtasya carati svadhābhiramartyo martyenā sayoniḥ ‖*) (Ṛ. Saṃ. 1-164-30)

Only in these two passages has Sāyaṇa given the word जीव (*jīva*) the meaning "the individual self (jīvātman)". He states its nature as connected with the body that dies, and as having the same abode as the living being that is liable to death. Quoting the Upaniṣad sentence जीवापेतं वाव किलेदं म्रियते, न जीवो म्रियते (*jīvāpetaṃ vāva kiledaṃ mriyate, na jīvo mriyate*) (Chā. U. 6-11-3) **NOTE**, he explains the difference between the self and the body. In the same way the words प्राण (*prāṇa*) and मनस् (*manas*) are also used in the sense of consciousness. Moreover,

द्वा सुपर्णा सयुजा सखाया समानं वृक्षं परि षष्वजाते । (*dvā suparṇā sayujā sakhāyā samānaṃ vṛkṣaṃ pari ṣaṣvajāte |*) (1-164-20)

Here he states that the word सुपर्ण (*suparṇa*) is a synonym of the individual self. Thus the use of various words conveys the eternal principle that is distinct from the body. On the whole, the seers who saw the sūktas, in the sentences of the Ṛksaṃhitā, state their views on the self thus:
1) In a person there is a part of consciousness that differs from the insentient.
2) It is beyond the body. It remains even after the body has perished.

### Printed p. 432
3) It is without birth and death, and everlasting.
4) In earthly life it is the vital essence of the body and the governor of the body's functions.
5) Whatever action it performs while in contact with the body in earthly life, it experiences the fruit of that action even after it is separated from the body. These and similar points they have made clear.

For a dead person there are three paths on which to go according to his own deeds: devayāna, pitṛyāna and narakayāna. (In the Ṛksaṃhitā the first two paths are clearly described; the third, narakayāna, is only hinted at by some descriptions.) Of these, the difference between the two paths devayāna and pitṛyāna was stated briefly earlier. What is to be understood in the present context is only this: which is the pitṛyāna, for whom is the state of pitṛ, and what is the nature of the Pitṛloka.

2) The groups of pitṛs; the Pitṛlokas

उदीरतामवर उत्परास उन्मध्यमाः पितरः सोम्यासः । असुं य ईयुरवृका ऋतज्ञास्ते नोऽवंतु पितरो हवेषु ॥ (*udīratāmavara utparāsa unmadhyamāḥ pitaraḥ somyāsaḥ | asuṃ ya īyuravṛkā ṛtajñāste no 'vaṃtu pitaro haveṣu ‖*) (Ṛ. Saṃ. 10-15-1)

In this mantra the Pitṛlokas are specified. त्रिविधाः पितर. उत्तमा मधमा अधमाश्चेति । (*trividhāḥ pitara. uttamā madhamā adhamāśceti |*) There are three kinds of groups of pitṛs: the highest, the middle and the lowest. All of them are described as knowers of ṛta (*ṛtajñāḥ*), and are prayed to protect all out of compassion. But how their pitṛhood arises is hard to state precisely. Did they all first take human birth on earth and then, as the fruit of their good rites, reach the Pitṛloka after death? Or have they been in these worlds from beginningless time? Do they also have a divine element? And so on. Many are described as having attained divinity and as dwelling in the highest divine world. Besides this, dividing the three kinds of groups of pitṛs, the Śatapatha indicates these groups as follows:

तद्ये सोमेनीजानाः। ते पितरो सोमवंतोथ ये दत्तेन पक्वेन लोकं जयंति ते पितरो बर्हिषदोथ ये ततो नान्यतरश्चन यानग्निरेव दहन्स्‌द्वयति ते पितरोग्निष्वात्ता एत उ ये ते पितरः ॥ (*tadye somenījānāḥ| te pitaro somavaṃtotha ye dattena pakvena lokaṃ jayaṃti te pitaro barhiṣadotha ye tato nānyataraścana yānagnireva dahansdvayati te pitarogniṣvāttā eta u ye te pitaraḥ ‖*) (Śa. Brā. 2.6-1-7)

The pitṛs who performed the sacrifice offering soma are the Somavantas. Those who won the world of the gods by cooked offerings such as the puroḍāśa are the Barhiṣads. Those who have neither of these, and were burned by fire alone,

### Printed p. 433
are the Agniṣvāttas. Thus the pitṛs are specified in three divisions. These names accord with their rites. So the scheme of dividing the groups of pitṛs is of two kinds. If the above division in the śrāddha section is examined, the pitṛs described as परासः (*parāsaḥ*) possess an exceedingly divine nature.

अंगिरसो नः पितरो नवग्वा अथर्वाणो भृगवः सोम्यासः ॥ (*aṃgiraso naḥ pitaro navagvā atharvāṇo bhṛgavaḥ somyāsaḥ ‖*) (Ṛ. Saṃ. 10-14.6)

The Ṛbhus, Maruts, Aṅgirases, Virūpas, Navagvas, Daśagvas, Atharvans, Bhṛgus and Kuśikas all belong to this group. All of them obtained divinity by their excellent deeds, became immortal, and like the gods are worthy of worship.

इंद्रस्य सख्यमृभवः समानशुर्मनोर्नपातो अपसो दधन्विरे । सौधन्वनासो अमृतत्वमेरिरे विष्ट्वी शमीभिः सुकृतः सुकृत्यया ॥ (*iṃdrasya sakhyamṛbhavaḥ samānaśurmanornapāto apaso dadhanvire | saudhanvanāso amṛtatvamerire viṣṭvī śamībhiḥ sukṛtaḥ sukṛtyayā ‖*) (Ṛ. Saṃ. 3-60-3)

The Ṛbhus, who belonged to the group of men and were sons of Sudhanvan, performed excellent sacrificial rites and attained friendship with Indra. The praise that the Ṛbhus, sons of Sudhanvan, obtained divinity and freedom from death by their excellent deeds is repeated in many places in different forms (4-35-8 and others).

तेवर्धंत स्वतवसो महित्वना नाकं तस्थुरुरु चक्रिरे सदः । विष्णुर्यद्धावद्वृषणं मदच्युतं वयो न सीदन्नधि बर्हिषि प्रिये ॥ (*tevardhaṃta svatavaso mahitvanā nākaṃ tasthururu cakrire sadaḥ | viṣṇuryaddhāvadvṛṣaṇaṃ madacyutaṃ vayo na sīdannadhi barhiṣi priye ‖*) (Ṛ. Saṃ. 1-85-7)

The Maruts, who move by their own power and have exceeding greatness, have climbed to the heavenly world and obtained the right to dwell there. May such Maruts favour us.

ये यज्ञेन दक्षिणया समक्ता इंद्रस्य सख्यममृतत्वमानश । तेभ्यो भद्रमंगिरसो वो अस्तु प्रति गृभीत मानवं सुमेधसः ॥ (*ye yajñena dakṣiṇayā samaktā iṃdrasya sakhyamamṛtatvamānaśa | tebhyo bhadramaṃgiraso vo astu prati gṛbhīta mānavaṃ sumedhasaḥ ‖*) (Ṛ. Saṃ. 10.62.1)

O Aṅgirases, who, joined with sacrificial oblations and with fees (dakṣiṇā), worshipped the gods: by your good deeds you obtained Indra's friendship. For that very reason freedom from death came to you also. O Aṅgirases, doers of good deeds and attainers of a good destination, favour us. Thus the occasions on which the Ṛbhus, Maruts and Aṅgirases also attained divinity are stated. In the same way,
xxvii 28

मक्षू कनायाः सख्यं नवग्वा ऋतं वदंत ऋतयुक्तिमग्मन् । (*makṣū kanāyāḥ sakhyaṃ navagvā ṛtaṃ vadaṃta ṛtayuktimagman |*) (10-61-10)

By such sentences the greatness of the seers belonging to the groups of pitṛs, the Navagvas, Daśagvas, Bhṛgus and others, is praised. It is probably described that all of these possess the divine radiance of Āditya and are protected by deities such as Pūṣan, who are connected with the sun. Pūṣan is also prayed to be the protector of the departed who go to and reach that world.

आयुर्विश्वायुः परि पासति त्वा पूषा त्वा पातु प्रपथे पुरस्तात् । यत्रासते सुकृतो यत्र ते ययुस्तत्र त्वा देवः सविता दधातु ॥ (*āyurviśvāyuḥ pari pāsati tvā pūṣā tvā pātu prapathe purastāt | yatrāsate sukṛto yatra te yayustatra tvā devaḥ savitā dadhātu ‖*) (Ṛ. Saṃ. 10-17-4)

"May Vāyu, the inner controller of all, protect you. May the god Pūṣan protect you as you go on the excellent path of heaven. Where the excellent pitṛs are, who earlier obtained the excellent world by their divine deeds, there may Savitṛ place you." Thus the connection of the sun with the excellent world of these pitṛs is stated. Some mantras quoted below show the connection between the pitṛs belonging to the highest group and Āditya, who dwells in the highest, radiant world.

आ भरतं शिक्षतं वज्रबाहू अस्मा इंद्राग्नी अवतं शचीभिः । इमे सु ते रश्मयः सूर्यस्य येभिः सपित्वं पितरो न आसन् ॥ (*ā bharataṃ śikṣataṃ vajrabāhū asmā iṃdrāgnī avataṃ śacībhiḥ | ime su te raśmayaḥ sūryasya yebhiḥ sapitvaṃ pitaro na āsan ‖*) (Ṛ. Saṃ. 1-10) **NOTE**
(Ṛ. Saṃ. 1-109-7)

उच्चा दिवि दक्षिणावंतो अस्थुर्यै अश्वदाः सह ते सूर्येण । हिरण्यदा अमृतत्वं भजंते वासोदाः सोम प्रतिरंतु आयुः ॥ (*uccā divi dakṣiṇāvaṃto asthuryai aśvadāḥ saha te sūryeṇa | hiraṇyadā amṛtatvaṃ bhajaṃte vāsodāḥ soma pratiraṃtu āyuḥ ‖*) (10-107-2)

सहस्रणीथाः कवयो ये गोपायंति सूर्यं । ऋषीन् तपस्वतो यम तपोजा अपि गच्छतात् ॥ (*sahasraṇīthāḥ kavayo ye gopāyaṃti sūryaṃ | ṛṣīn tapasvato yama tapojā api gacchatāt ‖*) (10-154-29)

With whichever rays of Āditya our pitṛs, doers of excellent deeds, attained union, and with those rays reached the world of Brahmā, may those rays favour us. Those who gave fees generously in the sacrificial rite have reached the excellent world. Those who gave the gift of a horse have reached the world of the sun. Those who have done such excellent deeds are able to protect even Āditya. "O Yama, take the ascetic seers to such an excellent world"—thus it is prayed, and so on.

Those divine women, like the Aṅgirases, cooked in the lap of the earth. With their help he too now cooks. The divine women who in former times honoured the gods through their excellent works are the very ones who now shine in the form of stars. The fathers who in former times attained divinity and reached the atmosphere are the ones who now shine as stars. It is praised that those very stars are helping this sacrificer also.

On the whole, the description of these fathers who attained divinity is the most abundant. Their world may, from a gross point of view, be called the world of Yama. (But, by showing the identity of Yama and Āditya in many contexts, it was stated earlier, when Yama was being explained, that the world of Āditya is itself the world of Yama.) This lower world of theirs consists of the worlds of the fathers who performed ordinary good works. But the other two worlds are the ones that are praised more. The description and praise of these most excellent worlds is as follows.

> यत्र ज्योतिरजस्रं यस्मिल्लोके स्पर्धितं ।

(Ṛ. Saṃ. 9-113.7)

> यत्र राजा वैवस्वतो यत्रावरोधनं दिवः ।
> यत्रामूरह्वतीरापस्तत्र माममृतं कृधींद्रायेंदो परि स्रव ॥
> यत्रानुकामं चरणं त्रिनाके त्रिदिवे दिवः ।
> लोका यत्र ज्योतिष्मंतस्तत्र मामृतं कृधींद्रायेंदो परि स्रव ॥
> यत्र कामा निकामाश्च यत्र ब्रध्नस्य विष्टपं ।
> स्वधा च यत्र तृप्तिश्च तत्र मामृतं कृधींद्रायेंदो परि स्रव ॥
> यत्रानंदाश्च मोदाश्च मुदः प्रमुद आसते ।
> कामस्य यत्राप्राः कामास्तत्र माममृतं कृधींद्रायेंदो परि स्रव ॥
> कामस्य यत्राप्राः कामास्तत्र माममृतं कृधींद्रायेंदो परि स्रव ॥

(Ṛ. Saṃ. 8. 113 8-11)**NOTE**

In the world where Āditya is established and the divine light shines eternally; where Yama, son of Vivasvat, is the lord; where there is the inner dwelling of Āditya; where there are eternal streams of water; in the third region, the heaven-world, where Āditya moves about as he wishes; where there is eternal bliss; where there is well-being and the satisfaction of desires and eternal bliss, there make me immortal — thus the prayer is made.

### Printed p. 436

This place, a bliss-giving abode for the Aṅgirases, the Ṛbhus and others, is the most excellent supreme place. Those who dwell here are the ones indicated by the word परासः (*parāsaḥ*). As soon as they leave the body that rests on the earth they obtain divine light and go to that world either in a chariot or by means of wings. (A. Ve. 11. 1. 37)**NOTE** Sometimes the Maruts too carry such beings. (A. Ve. 18. 2. 21-6)**NOTE** Passages such as सं गच्छस्व पितृभिः (*saṃ gacchasva pitṛbhiḥ*) (Ṛ. Saṃ. 10-14-8) show that the world of Yama, king of the fathers, is the destined place of these dead.

> अनतिप्रश्नां मा देवतामत्यप्राक्षीः पुरेतिथ्यै मरिष्यसि न तेस्थीनि चन
> गृहान् प्राप्स्यंतीति .... ....

(Ca. Brā. 11. 6. 3. 11)**NOTE**

Passages such as this show the connection between the burning of the dead body and the going of the departed spirits to the divine world of Yama. These accounts apply only to beings who performed the most excellent good works. But what is the course of the other beings? What paths do they travel after death? These matters too must now be examined.

When the dead go to the world of Yama, they have to cross there the Sārameyas (dogs), which have four eyes and long noses and are terrible. The departed is instructed to cross those terrible Sārameyas and quickly reach the presence of Yama. It is also stated that those same dogs protect the departed who have gone to Yama and joined him. यमसंबुधिनौ श्वानौ प्रेतस्य बाधकौ तौ परित्यज्य समीचीनेन मार्गेण प्रेतं नय (*yamasaṃbudhinau śvānau pretasya bādhakau tau parityajya samīcīnena mārgeṇa pretaṃ naya*): Agni is prayed to lead the departed to Yama, taking him across the dogs of Yama that harm the departed. (Ṛ. Saṃ. 10-14-10). And ताभ्यामेनं परि देहि (*tābhyāmenaṃ pari dehi*) (10-14-11): Yama is prayed to hand this departed one over to those dogs for his protection. Moreover, उरूणसावसुतृपा उदंबलौ यमस्य दूतौ चरतो जना अनु (*urūṇasāvasutṛpā udaṃbalau yamasya dūtau carato janā anu*) (10-14-12): the description that those dogs, fattened by sucking the blood of living beings, always move about with their eyes on living beings, also shows their terrible form. Since these two points are stated, the purport may be that they protect doers of good works and harm doers of bad works. (What the true nature of those Sārameyas may be has been stated earlier.)

But the matter of precedence for doers of good and punishment for doers of evil is nowhere stated precisely in the Ṛksaṃhitā.

### Printed p. 437

Only in places such as यद्दक्षिणो वेद्यंतः स यत्साधु करोति तदंतर्वेद्यथ यदसाधु (*yaddakṣiṇo vedyaṃtaḥ sa yatsādhu karoti tadaṃtarvedyatha yadasādhu*) (Śa. Brā. 11-2-7-33) is this difference clearly stated. What good state is attained by the righteous and what happiness they have there has been explained above. The unrighteous do not have this status. As to what fruit they obtain: it is arrival in hell. The Ṛksaṃhitā does not describe the nature of hell as the Purāṇas and other works do. Even so, situations are described in which they have no good state and are to be thrust into a dark nether world. Only a few of these are cited here.

> अभ्रातरो न योषणो व्यंतः पतिरिपो न जनयो दुरेवाः ।
> पापासः संतो अनृता असत्या इदं पदमजनता गभीरं ॥

(Ṛ. Saṃ. 4-5-5)

In this verse the world obtained by the most sinful is declared to be a deep, dark world. The suffering that befalls along with it is also described. May the greatest suffering come upon people who are of false mind, untruthful, and who have practised other kinds of sin. Like a helpless woman without protectors, and like a woman hated by her husband, may these sinful beings wander without refuge in this darkness.

> इंद्रा सोमा दुष्कृतो वव्रे अंतरनारंभणे तमसि प्र विध्यतं ।
> यथा नातः पुनरेकश्चनोदयत्तद्वामस्तु सहसे मन्युमच्छवः ॥

(Ṛ. Saṃ. 7. 104. 3)

O Indra and Soma, thrust the wicked rākṣasas, who led an evil life, into the bottomless dark world. May not one of them rise up again, and so on. Although in such prayers there is the idea of hell, it is not clear that this is the fixed place for the departed dead.

As described in the Ṛksaṃhitā passages, the sinful are all those who do not perform sacrificial rites.

*adevayuḥ* — those who do not perform worship of the gods and the like as prescribed.
ब्रह्मद्विषः (*brahmadviṣaḥ*) — those who revile hymns of praise and those who praise.
अव्रताः (*avratāḥ*) — those without sacrificial and other rites.
असुन्वतः (*asunvataḥ*), अप्पणतः (*appaṇataḥ*), अशसः (*aśasaḥ*) — those who do not offer oblations such as Soma; those who do not recite hymns of praise.**NOTE**

All these are regarded as the most sinful. They may belong to the group of humans or to the group of asuras and the like. For all of them many

### Printed p. 438

kinds of punishments are prescribed. "O Agni, do not favour those without rites, and punish such people" — thus Agni and all the other gods are prayed to. (1. 150. 2; 3. 18. 2; 10. 38. 3 etc.). Just as freedom, which brings happiness, is described for doers of meritorious works, so for the most sinful bondage, which brings suffering, is described in the same manner. The words पाश (*pāśa*), रज्जु (*rajju*), प्रसति (*prasati*), बंध (*baṃdha*) and the like denote such bondage. Just as happiness and freedom are possible in worlds such as heaven, so this bondage must be experienced in a world corresponding to it. The words वव्र (*vavra*), गाध (*gādha*), तमः (*tamaḥ*) and the like indicate the nature of this world. The use of the words वव्र (*vavra*) and गभीर (*gabhīra*) and their purport are shown in the mantras cited above. (Ṛ. Saṃ. 4. 5. 5; 7. 104. 3). These indicate only a world full of darkness. That which is the opposite of the heaven-world is the hell-world — this is stated precisely only in the Atharvaveda. (A. Ve. 12. 4. 36).**NOTE** The description of this hell-world is also clear in a Ṛksaṃhitā passage.

> वि न इंद्र मृधो जहि नीचा यच्छ हृतन्यतः ।
> यो अस्मा अभिधासत्यधरं गमया तमः ॥

(10. 152. 4)

O Indra, destroy those who harm us. Thrust downward those who wish to fight us. Send whichever enemy attacks us most fiercely to the lowest, deepest pit of darkness, and so on. But there is no description of terrible fire connected with hell, nor any account of other tortures.

Some Western scholars, explaining this point, say that the word वीची (*vīcī*) is a synonym of hell.

> बृहन्मित्रस्य वरुणस्य धाम कदु ब्रव आहनो वीच्या न्हान् ।

(10-10-6)

Here Sāyaṇa too has explained वीच्या (*vīcyā*) as meaning नरकेण (*narakeṇa*). The tortures of hell are described clearly in the Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa.

Bhṛgu, following the direction of his father Varuṇa, travels in the four directions, observing the departed spirits who undergo experiences according to their works, and sees extremely horrible sights: men cutting men to pieces, tearing and eating one another, and similar scenes are described. All these are the torments of hell. In the Jaiminīya Brāhmaṇa

### Printed p. 439

three kinds of heavens and three kinds of hells are set out. (Jai. Brā. 1-42-43-44).**NOTE** The Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa makes clear that good reward for good works and bad experience for bad works are assured in heaven and hell. (Śa. Brā. 6-2-2-27 and 10-6-3-1 etc.).

For reaching heaven and the other worlds, the man's own action alone is not the means. The rite performed on the dead body is also one of these means.

> स एवंविदा दह्यमानः सहैव धूमेन स्वर्गलोकमेतीति विज्ञायते ।

(Āśvalāyana Gṛhya Sūtra 4-4-7)

It is said that only if he is burnt as prescribed does the person within that body go to heaven; but in the Ṛksaṃhitā no such rule is laid down anywhere. It is described that all of them, whether burnt by fire or not burnt by fire, sit in heaven and are satisfied with svadhā (Ṛ. Saṃ. 10-15-14). The view that the earth is the support of the dead man's body is also stated in many places.

> पितृणाग्ं सदनमसीति बर्हिरव स्तृणाति पितृदेवत्या २ ग्ग् हैतद्यन्निखातं

(Tai. Saṃ. 6-3-4-2)

> शुंधंतां लोकाः पितृषदना इति पितृदेवत्यो वै कूपः खातस्तमेवैतन्मेध्यं करोति ॥

(Śa. Brā. 3-6-1-13)

The pit dug near the sacrificial altar for the rite is most excellent. This pit is the dwelling place of the fathers, and so on; it is described thus in many places. The rice-balls and other offerings made to the departed are not offered in fire to be carried to heaven. In many contexts the earth is dug and they are put into the pit. But there is a difference between the balls offered at the śrāddha and those offered immediately after death. A man does not go to heaven and join the world of the fathers immediately upon dying. The śrāddha to be performed up to one year after death, and its resolve, are different. It also differs from the balls offered to father, grandfather, great-grandfather and the like. There is a belief that for one year the spirit of the dead remains near the earth. But the Ṛksaṃhitā does not state this distinction. As soon as he dies the man certainly joins the former fathers. Even if there is a difference between a father and the state of a departed spirit, there is no support for the idea that the dead man has come to the earth in the form of a bhūta (piśāca) for the fulfilment of his desires; it is only described that the fathers come to the earth to receive śrāddha and the like.

### Printed p. 440

> इदं पितृभ्यो नमो अस्त्वद्य ये पूर्वासो य उपरास ईयुः ।
> ये पार्थिवे रजस्या निषत्ता ये वा नूनं सुवृजनासु विक्षु ॥

(Ṛ. Saṃ. 10. 15. 2)

May our homage be offered to the fathers who have gone and joined the world of the fathers. Whether they were older than we by birth, or younger than we, after death, having joined the world of the fathers, they are venerable to us all. May our homage be offered to such fathers, and to the fathers who have come to the earthly world at the time of our śrāddha — thus the fathers who have come to the earth are indicated.

Moreover, if certain sinful acts are committed, there is no attainment of the world of the fathers for a fixed time. For example:

> इति योऽपगुरातै शतेन यातयाद्यो निहनत्सहस्रेण यातयाद्यो
> लोहितं शरवद्यावतः प्रस्कद्य पाग्ं सून्त्यंगृह्णात्तावतस्संवत्सरान् पितृ
> लोकं न प्रजानादिति ॥

(Kṛ. Saṃ. 2. 6. 10. 2).**NOTE**

Those who strike, hurt and fell venerable persons: if such people die, they do not at once attain the excellent world. For as many years as the number of grains of sand moistened by the drops of blood that fall to the ground, the spirits of those dead cannot reach the world of the fathers; they must wander in the earthly world itself. But they cannot be called piśācas as described in the Purāṇas and elsewhere. Even though the word पैशाच (*paiśāca*) occurs in Vedic passages, it should be understood as an evil power belonging to the group of rākṣasas and the like.

3. Rebirth and transmigration

According to some scholars there is no basis in the Ṛksaṃhitā for the view that a man who has died takes an earthly body again and is born on the earth. Others argue that there are passages indicating that rebirth is self-evident. Along with the directions that his spirit must reach heaven or hell according to his works, whether there are passages in the Saṃhitās prescribing that he be born again on the earth according to each one's works is the matter to be examined in the present context.

> सं गच्छस्व पितृभिः सं यमेनेष्टापूर्तेन परमे व्योमन् ।
> हित्वायावद्यं पुनरस्तमेहि संगच्छस्व तन्वा सुवर्चाः ॥

(Ṛ. Saṃ. 10-14-8)

### Printed p. 441
…in which the departed one is addressed. It is told that he, united with the Pitṛs, enjoys in the highest world the fruit that accords with his deeds, and takes up a body suited to it. What does *tanvā* mean here? There is a discussion whether it means a divine body or again an earthly body. Sāyaṇa has explained *ehi* as "come" (आगच्छ (*āgaccha*)). No one can call the departed "come again to this world". Therefore on the strength of this sentence no definite view can be stated about rebirth in the earthly world. And further:

सूर्यं चक्षुर्गच्छतु वातमात्मा द्यां च गच्छ पृथिवीं च धर्मणा । अपो वा गच्छ यदि तत्र ते हितमोषधीषु प्रति तिष्ठा शरीरैः । (*sūryaṃ cakṣurgacchatu vātamātmā dyāṃ ca gaccha pṛthivīṃ ca dharmaṇā | apo vā gaccha yadi tatra te hitamoṣadhīṣu prati tiṣṭhā śarīraiḥ |*) (Ṛ. Saṃ. 10-16-3)

O departed one, may your eye go to the sun; may your breath go to the wind. According to the fruit of your deeds go to the heavenly world, or to the earth, or to the atmosphere. Be united with limbs in the form of plants. Such sentences speak of birth again in the earthly world. But views such as return and rebirth are not stated definitely. This discussion also is not much to the point in this context. This matter, which has arisen incidentally, is only indicated to some extent. If the occasion arises later, the subject will be examined.

**4. The funeral rite for the departed**

After a man has died, one of two rites must be performed: burning the body or burying it. Some hold, from statements such as अग्निदग्धाः अनग्निदग्धाः (*agnidagdhāḥ anagnidagdhāḥ*) (Ṛ. Saṃ. 10-15-14), that both practices were in use. But merely because अनग्निदग्धाः (*anagnidagdhāḥ*) occurs, it cannot be said that this custom was regularly in force. Sāyaṇa has explained this word as श्मशानकर्मरहिताः (*śmaśānakarmarahitāḥ*) ("without the cremation-ground rite"). Where some mishap occurs and there is no opportunity for any rite, the departed has no cremation-ground rite. Therefore it cannot be said on this basis alone that this custom too was in practice. Whether, like the rite of burning, the custom of burying in the earth was also current, must be examined: is there any other support in the Saṃhitā sentences?

उप सर्प मातरं भूमिमेतामुरुव्यचसं पृथिवीं सुशेवां । ऊर्णम्रदा युवतिर्दक्षिणावत एषा त्वा पातु निर्यतेरुपस्थात् ॥ (*upa sarpa mātaraṃ bhūmimetāmuruvyacasaṃ pṛthivīṃ suśevāṃ | ūrṇamradā yuvatirdakṣiṇāvata eṣā tvā pātu niryaterupasthāt ‖*) (Ṛ. Saṃ. 10-18-10)

उत्ते स्तभ्नामि पृथिवीं त्वत्परीमं लोगं निदधन्मो अहं रिषं । एतां स्थूणां पितरो धारयंतु तेऽत्रा यमः सादना! ते मिनोतु ॥ (*utte stabhnāmi pṛthivīṃ tvatparīmaṃ logaṃ nidadhanmo ahaṃ riṣaṃ | etāṃ sthūṇāṃ pitaro dhārayaṃtu te 'trā yamaḥ sādanā! te minotu ‖*) (Ṛ. Saṃ. 10-18-13)

### Printed p. 442
O dead body, enter this broad earth. This earth is a giver of comfort. She gives a shelter soft as wool. She gives protection from Nirṛti to the excellent sacrificer. Therefore enter her without fear.

O dead body, I push a heap of earth around you. Let no harm come to you. Let no power harm me either. Let the Pitṛs be your supporters. Let Yama make an excellent dwelling for you. In such ways the circumstances of placing the body in the earth like a deposit are described clearly.

माता पुत्रं यथा सिचाभ्येनं भूम ऊर्णुहि (*mātā putraṃ yathā sicābhyenaṃ bhūma ūrṇuhi*) (Ṛ. Saṃ. 10-18-11)

As a mother covers her child with a fine wrapper, so this Mother Earth covers the dead body and gives it protection; thus the safety of the dead body is praised.

Whether the dead body is burned or buried, there are also many rites to be performed before that. If the householder worshipped the consecrated fire before death, the dead body is to be placed near that very fire, purified with cow-dung and covered with seats of darbha grass. There are many proofs that the same rites were in practice in the earlier tradition, in the prescribed manner, just as the injunctions are found in the later Gṛhya Sūtras and the like. (The details of these are not to the point at present.) With the recital of mantras such as अपेत नीत वि च सर्पतातः (*apeta nīta vi ca sarpatātaḥ*) the body is to be conveyed by its relatives as far as the cremation ground. But whether the body was carried on the shoulders or taken on a chariot or the like cannot be said definitely. After going to the cremation ground, the body is to be offered on the fire-pile. If he had worshipped the three fires while alive, the pile is to be in the cremation ground too, in the midst of fires kindled from portions of the household fires (the Dakṣiṇāgni, the Gārhapatya and the Āhavanīya). For the sake of the rite his wife is laid beside him, and then she is told to rise from there.

उदीर्ष्य नारभि जीवलोकं गतासुमेतमुप शेष एहि । हस्तग्राभस्य दिधिषोस्तवेदं पत्युर्जनित्वमभि सं बभूव ॥ (*udīrṣya nārabhi jīvalokaṃ gatāsumetamupa śeṣa ehi | hastagrābhasya didhiṣostavedaṃ patyurjanitvamabhi saṃ babhūva ‖*) (Ṛ. Saṃ. 10-18-8)

O woman, wife of the dead man, you have lain down on the couch beside this husband who took your hand and resolved to die with him. But rise from here, come, and join your sons and others who are living — thus she is directed. After that follow the traditions of the piling of the fire and the like.

### Printed p. 443
There are proofs that even in preparing the pile for the burning rite a digging rite was performed. Thus:

अथैतां दिशमग्नीन् नयंति (*athaitāṃ diśamagnīn nayaṃti*) । (यस्यां दिशि भूमिभागः खानितः तां दिशमग्नीन् नयंति (*yasyāṃ diśi bhūmibhāgaḥ khānitaḥ tāṃ diśamagnīn nayaṃti*)) (Ā. Gṛ. Sū. 4-2-1) **NOTE**

It says that the fire is to be carried to the region where the fire-pile has been made. At that fire-piling, barhis is to be spread and the wife is to be seated to the north of it: उत्तरतः पत्नीं (*uttarataḥ patnīṃ*) (संवेशयंति (*saṃveśayaṃti*)) (Ā. Gṛ. Sū. 4.2-13). After the wife has been given the direction described above, the fire is to be offered with the actions proper to the respective varṇa. The details of the other rites are not to the point at present. But only some traditions that reflect the Vedic culture may be examined here. By the mantras to be recited at this rite, the protection of the departed one, who has died at the time of the funeral rite, must necessarily be entrusted to Agni. Agni is prayed to carry this departed one to his appointed place without harming him. The course of that prayer is as follows.

मैनमग्ने वि दहो माभि शोचो मास्य त्वचं चिक्षिपो मा शरीरं । यदा शृतं कृणवो जातवेदोऽथेमेनं प्र हिणुतात्पितृभ्यः ॥ (*mainamagne vi daho mābhi śoco māsya tvacaṃ cikṣipo mā śarīraṃ | yadā śṛtaṃ kṛṇavo jātavedo 'themenaṃ pra hiṇutātpitṛbhyaḥ ‖*) (Ṛ. Saṃ. 10-16-1)

O Agni, do not burn him up entirely. Do not harm him. Do not let his body scatter. When you have burned his body fully, he is to be carried to the Pitṛs. After he is fully cooked, this departed one reaches the world of the Pitṛs according to the resolve of the gods. May his eye join the sun. May his self join the wind. O departed one, according to your deeds go to the heavenly world or to the earth. Or dwell in the water or in plants and the like. O Agni, burn up all the parts of the body that remain unburnt. May your radiance burn those parts completely.

इममग्ने चमसं मा वि जिह्वरः प्रियो देवानुमुत सोम्यानां । एष यश्चमसो देवपानस्तस्मिन्देवा अमृता मादयंते ॥ (*imamagne camasaṃ mā vi jihvaraḥ priyo devānumuta somyānāṃ | eṣa yaścamaso devapānastasmindevā amṛtā mādayaṃte ‖*) (Ṛ. Saṃ. 10-16-8)

O Agni, do not shake this cup (camasa) filled with soma, offered here for the Pitṛs who love soma and for the gods. It is a vessel fit for the gods' drinking. By drinking from it the immortal gods rejoice. Thus at the time of the fire-piling there are many prayers for the welfare of the departed. Last of all:

### Printed p. 444
अस्मात्त्वमधि जातोऽसि त्वदयं जायतां पुनः । आसौ स्वर्गाय लोकाय स्वाहा ॥ (*asmāttvamadhi jāto 'si tvadayaṃ jāyatāṃ punaḥ | āsau svargāya lokāya svāhā ‖*) (Śa. Brā. ga-5-2-15) **NOTE**

O Agni, from him you were born (in the form of the sacrificial fire). By you, so born, may he obtain birth in the excellent divine world — such is the final prayer.

After the fire-piling, the relatives of the dead man withdraw from that place without looking back: इत्यनपेक्षामेत्यप उपस्पृशंति (*ityanapekṣāmetyapa upaspṛśaṃti*) (Śa. Brā. 12-5-2.15). They bathe and perform the remaining rites. (That description too is not to the point at present.) Here another point is noteworthy. There are many proofs that the belief that the dead man, in the form of a departed spirit, wanders for ten days near his relatives has grown up continuously since Vedic times. Purification comes only after the gathering of the bones and the other rites have been performed; till then there is no purification.

The belief that the memorial built in remembrance of the dead man, and the rites to be performed at that memorial, bring satisfaction to the dead man's spirit is also seen in the Vedic tradition.

अथास्मै कल्याणं कुर्वंति । अथास्मै स्मशानं कुर्वंति । गृहान् वा प्रज्ञानं वा यो वै कश्च म्रियते स शवस्तस्मा एतदन्नं करोति...... .... ......॥ (*athāsmai kalyāṇaṃ kurvaṃti | athāsmai smaśānaṃ kurvaṃti | gṛhān vā prajñānaṃ vā yo vai kaśca mriyate sa śavastasmā etadannaṃ karoti...... .... ......‖*) (Śa. Brā. 13-8-1-1).

Then the dead man's kinsmen make efforts so that the departed one may attain a good state. They build a memorial for him. This is the place where food is offered to the dead man. Because it is the place where food is offered to a corpse, this place is also called *śmaśāna*. Or *śmaśana* is also a synonym of *Pitṛs*; since food prepared for them is offered here, it is understood that the name *śmaśāna* arises also from that. Dancing, the playing of instruments such as the flute and similar acts are performed. The belief that whatever things are pleasing to a man living on earth are pleasing also to the dead man is likewise beginningless. Therefore many things such as clothes, ornaments and fruit are offered for the satisfaction of the departed.

Besides the common rites performed for all the dead, certain still more extensive special rites are prescribed for excellent sacrificers. One who has performed the Agnihotra and a knower of Brahman (one who has performed the Brahmamedha) are eligible for special rites. If pregnant women die, a special rite is prescribed for them too. As in the present tradition, the head of an ascetic

### Printed p. 445
is pierced with a coconut so that his spirit leaves through that Brahmarandhra; this practice is not seen to have existed in the Vedic tradition.

Whatever earthly rite is performed for the satisfaction of the departed, the experience of pleasure and pain of the departed is fixed according to his own deeds. This point becomes clear from the difference of the two paths along which the spirit of the dead travels, called Pitṛyāna and Devayāna.

The course of the individual self (jīvātman) according to its deeds is of two kinds. The path by which a soul goes when it has done good deeds and obtains heaven and other worlds is called Devayāna; the path to be taken by one who has not done good deeds but is engaged in selfish and similar pursuits is called Pitṛyāna. In the Ṛk Saṃhitā too the word Devayāna is well known. For example:

परं मृत्यो अनु परेहि पंथां यस्ते स्व इतरो देवयानात् । चक्षुष्मते शृण्वते ते ब्रवीमि मा नः प्रजां रीरिषो मोत वीरान् । (*paraṃ mṛtyo anu parehi paṃthāṃ yaste sva itaro devayānāt | cakṣuṣmate śṛṇvate te bravīmi mā naḥ prajāṃ rīriṣo mota vīrān |*) (Ṛ. Saṃ. 10-18-1)

In Ṛks such as this, Devayāna is said to be a path free from death. It is well known that on this path Savitṛ leads the doers of good to the sinless world free from death.

ये ते पंथाः सवितः पूर्व्यासोरेणवः सुकृता अंतरिक्षे । तेभिर्नो अद्य पथिभिः सुगेभी रक्षा च नो अधि च ब्रूहि देव ॥ (*ye te paṃthāḥ savitaḥ pūrvyāsoreṇavaḥ sukṛtā aṃtarikṣe | tebhirno adya pathibhiḥ sugebhī rakṣā ca no adhi ca brūhi deva ‖*) (Ṛ. Saṃ. 1-35-11)

यत्रासते सुकृतो यत्र ते ययुस्तत्र त्वा देवः सविता दधातु । (*yatrāsate sukṛto yatra te yayustatra tvā devaḥ savitā dadhātu |*) (Ṛ. Saṃ. 10-17-4)

In Ṛks such as these, since Savitṛ is the god who leads the doers of good along the good path, he is prayed to lead the sacrificers, the doers of good, along that same path, which is pure, free from dust and free from death. In the Upaniṣads this path is called the path beginning with the flame (arcirādi). This path is described as one on which the doers of good who have reached Brahmaloka after death do not return:

तत्पुरुषोऽमानवः स एवान्यह्म गमयत्येष देवपथो ब्रह्मपथ एतेन प्रतिपद्यमाना इमं मानवमावर्तं नावर्तंते नावर्तंते । (*tatpuruṣo 'mānavaḥ sa evānyahma gamayatyeṣa devapatho brahmapatha etena pratipadyamānā imaṃ mānavamāvartaṃ nāvartaṃte nāvartaṃte |*) (Chā. U. 4-15-5) **NOTE**

The person of lightning (the non-human one) leads this doer of good to Brahmaloka. This is the way to Brahmaloka. Those who have reached Brahmaloka by this path do not return. This is certain — thus it says.

### Printed p. 446
The same idea is described in the same way in the Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad also, and is stated just as in the present Ṛk. There:

सूरद्वारेण ते विरजाः प्रयांति यत्रामृतः स पुरुषो ह्यव्ययात्मा । (*sūradvāreṇa te virajāḥ prayāṃti yatrāmṛtaḥ sa puruṣo hyavyayātmā |*) (Mu. U. 1.11) **NOTE**

— this is what is said in the sentences describing the door of the sun. For those who reach Brahmaloka by Devayāna there is no return. But even those who reach the moon-world by the smoke path (Pitṛyāna), though they are doers of good, enjoy their good deeds there, and when that ends they come again to the earth. There are many differing views in the descriptions of Devayāna and Pitṛyāna; they are not so necessary at present. In the present Ṛk it is told that one who is united with a body and performs deeds in accordance with his own impressions has two kinds of passage. In the Bṛhadāraṇyaka this is said:

वेत्तो देवयानस्य वा पथः प्रतिपदं पितृयाणस्य वा यत्कृता देवयानं वा पंथानं प्रतिपद्यंते पितृयाणं वापि ऋषेर्वचः श्रुतं द्वे सृती अशृणवं पितृणामहं देवानामुत मर्त्यानां ताभ्यामिदं विश्वमेजत्समेति यदंतरा पितरं मातरं च इति ॥ (*vetto devayānasya vā pathaḥ pratipadaṃ pitṛyāṇasya vā yatkṛtā devayānaṃ vā paṃthānaṃ pratipadyaṃte pitṛyāṇaṃ vāpi ṛṣervacaḥ śrutaṃ dve sṛtī aśṛṇavaṃ pitṛṇāmahaṃ devānāmuta martyānāṃ tābhyāmidaṃ viśvamejatsameti yadaṃtarā pitaraṃ mātaraṃ ca iti ‖*) (Bra. U. 6-2-2) **NOTE**

When Pravāhaṇa Jaibali asked Śvetaketu, "Do you know the path that leads to the world of the gods, or have you understood the path that leads to the world of the Pitṛs?", he said no. Then Jaibali taught the sage's words: "There is one path that carries to the world of the Pitṛs; there is one path that carries to the world of the gods. These two are the paths that mortals travel after death. On these paths, which lie beyond heaven and earth, all moving beings travel."

**5. Pitṛ-śrāddha**

Just as by performing sacrifice one offers oblations to the gods, satisfies them and seeks to obtain their favour, so one of the aims of the worship of the Pitṛs is to perform śrāddha and the like, offer piṇḍas and the like to the Pitṛs, and when they are satisfied, to obtain favour from them. Just as the gods are called to help in obtaining worldly wealth, the Pitṛs too are called.

स्वादुषंसदः पितरो वयोधाः कृच्छ्रश्रितः शक्तीवंतो गभीराः । चित्रसेना इषुबला अमृध्राः सतोवीरा उरवो व्रातसाहाः ॥ (*svāduṣaṃsadaḥ pitaro vayodhāḥ kṛcchraśritaḥ śaktīvaṃto gabhīrāḥ | citrasenā iṣubalā amṛdhrāḥ satovīrā uravo vrātasāhāḥ ‖*) (Ṛ. Saṃ. 6, 75. 9)

### Printed p. 447
ब्राह्मणासः पितरः सोम्यासः शिवे नो द्यावापृथिवी अनेहसा । (*brāhmaṇāsaḥ pitaraḥ somyāsaḥ śive no dyāvāpṛthivī anehasā |*) (Ṛ. Saṃ. 6. 75. 10)

In this verse the extraordinary power and generosity of the Pitṛs are declared. The protecting Pitṛs destroy enemies and distribute the enemies' food among their sons and others. The prayer is: may the Pitṛs, firm in resolve for the destruction of enemies, armed with sharp weapons and destroyers of foes, be our protectors, and may they bring us well-being. But before such a prayer, they must first be satisfied by offering them piṇḍas and the like. This satisfaction comes in one way on one occasion and in another way on another. There are the śrāddhas to be performed on death anniversaries, the tarpaṇas offered at the parva times, and the worship offered on other special days. Besides these, the worship of the Pitṛs must be performed regularly even on auspicious days such as weddings. On certain occasions, however, the father, grandfather and great-grandfather are invited together with the earlier Pitṛs such as Aṅgiras. At auspicious times, when the invitation is made, the Pitṛs are addressed as *nāndīmukha*, that is, those whose faces are joyful. Thus, from many rites such as the pārvaṇa-śrāddha, the nāndī-śrāddha (vṛddhi-śrāddha) and the pūrva-śrāddha, there arises the faith, existing from Vedic times, that the Pitṛs are satisfied. Some of these rites are prescribed in the Saṃhitās and other texts themselves; others are only hinted at there and are explained clearly in the Śrauta-sūtras and the like. Here only a few of the most important rites are described, and the rest are indicated briefly.

Some of the important śrāddhas are known as yajñas. Among them the Piṇḍa-pitṛyajña and the Mahāpitṛyajña are the most important. Describing the power of the Piṇḍa-pitṛyajña, the Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa narrates a historical episode as follows.

प्रजापतिं वै भूतान्युपासीदन् । प्रजा वै भूतानि वि नो धेहि यथा जीवा मेति ततो देवा यज्योपवीतिनो भूत्वा दक्षिणं जान्वाच्योपासीदंस्थानब्रवीद्यज्ञो वोऽन्नममृतत्वं व ऊर्ग्वः सूरो वा ज्योतिरिति ॥ (*prajāpatiṃ vai bhūtānyupāsīdan | prajā vai bhūtāni vi no dhehi yathā jīvā meti tato devā yajyopavītino bhūtvā dakṣiṇaṃ jānvācyopāsīdaṃsthānabravīdyajño vo 'nnamamṛtatvaṃ va ūrgvaḥ sūro vā jyotiriti ‖*) (Śa. Brā. 2. 4. 2. 1)

Once all the beings created by Prajāpati approached Prajāpati and prayed: "O Father, teach us the way by which we may live." There were present the gods, the Pitṛs, human beings and the other creatures. Of these, the gods came first; wearing the sacred thread, with the right knee set on the ground, they approached Prajāpati. Then Prajāpati addressed the gods: "Sacrifice is your food, immortality is your essence, the Sun is your radiance."

### Printed p. 448
अथैनं पितरः । प्राचीनावीतिनः सव्यं जान्वाच्योपासीदंस्तानब्रवीन्मासिमासि वोशनग् स्वधा वो मनोजवोवश्चंद्रमा वो ज्योतिरिति ॥ (*athainaṃ pitaraḥ | prācīnāvītinaḥ savyaṃ jānvācyopāsīdaṃstānabravīnmāsimāsi vośanag svadhā vo manojavovaścaṃdramā vo jyotiriti ‖*) (Śa. Brā. 2. 4. 2. 2)

Then the Pitṛs, wearing the prācīnāvīti (the sacred thread on the right shoulder), with the left knee set on the ground, approached Prajāpati. Prajāpati addressed them: may you receive food every month; may the food called svadhā that is offered to you be the source of your mind-swiftness; the Moon is your light. So he blessed them and sent them away. (Afterwards he instructed human beings and the others, each according to its nature, and sent them away.)

The rite performed, as thus laid down by Prajāpati, to offer food in the form of svadhā to the Pitṛs every month at the parva time is called the Piṇḍa-pitṛyajña. This sacrifice is to be performed in the dakṣiṇāgni. The wearing of the sacred thread must be in the prācīnāvīti manner. Every act is to be done in the reverse (apradakṣiṇa) order. Together with the Pitṛs, Soma and Agni, the carrier of kavya, are invoked. (The description of the remaining ritual details is not relevant here.) It is believed that the oblation in the form of svadhā offered in this rite gives the Pitṛs the highest satisfaction. Similarly, the Mahāpitṛyajña is also very excellent and powerful, and its greatness is praised in many places. The Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa praises its power as follows.

महाहविषा ह वै देवा वृत्रं जघ्नुः । ते नो एव व्यजयंत येयमेषां विजितिस्तामथ यानेवैषां तस्मिन्त्संग्रामे अग्नंस्तान्पितृयज्ञेन समैरयंत पितरो वै त आसंस्तस्मात्पितृयज्ञो नाम । (*mahāhaviṣā ha vai devā vṛtraṃ jaghnuḥ | te no eva vyajayaṃta yeyameṣāṃ vijitistāmatha yānevaiṣāṃ tasmintsaṃgrāme agnaṃstānpitṛyajñena samairayaṃta pitaro vai ta āsaṃstasmātpitṛyajño nāma |*) (Śa. Brā. 2. 6. 1. 1)

With the great oblation the gods slew Vṛtra. By this very oblation they have attained their present powerful position. Afterwards they performed the Pitṛyajña and made all those who had died in the battle live again. Those who lived again there are the Pitṛs. For that very reason this sacrifice is well known by the name Mahāpitṛyajña.

तद्वसंतो ग्रीष्मो वर्षाः । एते ते ये व्यजयंत शरद्धेमंतः शिशिरस्त उ ते यान्पुनः समैरयंत ॥ (*tadvasaṃto grīṣmo varṣāḥ | ete te ye vyajayaṃta śaraddhemaṃtaḥ śiśirasta u te yānpunaḥ samairayaṃta ‖*) (Śa. Brā. 2. 6. 1. 2)

Spring, summer and the rainy season are the seasons that destroyed Vṛtra. Autumn, the cold season (hemanta) and winter (śiśira) are the seasons that brought the dead back to life. **NOTE**

### Printed p. 449
अथ यदेष एतेन यजते । तन्नाह नैवैतस्य तथा कंचन घ्नंतीति देवा अकुर्वन्निति नैवैष एतत्करोति यमुचैवैभ्यो देवा भागमकल्पयं. स्तमु चैवैभ्य एष यद्भागं करोति यानु चैव देवाः सम्मैरयंत तानु चैवैतदवति स्वानु चैवैतत्प्रित्यन् श्रेयाग्ं स लोकमुपोन्नयति यदु चैवास्यात्रात्मनोऽचरणेन हन्यते वा मीयते वा तदुचैवा सैतेन पुनराप्यायते तस्माद्वा एष एतेन यजते ॥ (*atha yadeṣa etena yajate | tannāha naivaitasya tathā kaṃcana ghnaṃtīti devā akurvanniti naivaiṣa etatkaroti yamucaivaibhyo devā bhāgamakalpayaṃ. stamu caivaibhya eṣa yadbhāgaṃ karoti yānu caiva devāḥ sammairayaṃta tānu caivaitadavati svānu caivaitatprityan śreyāgṃ sa lokamuponnayati yadu caivāsyātrātmano 'caraṇena hanyate vā mīyate vā taducaivā saitena punarāpyāyate tasmādvā eṣa etena yajate ‖*) (Śa. Brā. 2. ?. 1. 3) **NOTE**

There are two purposes in performing this Pitṛyajña. First, by performing this sacrifice the asuras cannot harm any of the people belonging to the sacrificer; and second, the gods themselves also performed this sacrifice and worshipped the Pitṛs. And the same share that the gods set apart and offered to the Pitṛs by performing this sacrifice, the sacrificer too must offer. By doing so, he not only satisfies the Pitṛs who were revived by the gods, but also, as it were, provides them with a still better state; and whatever deficiency there may be in his other rites is set right by the performance of this rite. For all these reasons this Pitṛyajña should be performed.

स पितृभ्यः सोमवद्भ्यः । षट्कपालं पुरोडाशं निर्वपति सोमाय वा पितृमते षड्वा ऋतव ऋतवः पितरस्तस्मात् षट्कपालो भवति ॥ (*sa pitṛbhyaḥ somavadbhyaḥ | ṣaṭkapālaṃ puroḍāśaṃ nirvapati somāya vā pitṛmate ṣaḍvā ṛtava ṛtavaḥ pitarastasmāt ṣaṭkapālo bhavati ‖*) (Śa. Brā. 2-6-1-4)

At the time of this rite he offers a puroḍāśa on six potsherds (ṣaṭkapāla) to the Pitṛs who possess Soma. (It may be meant "to Soma together with the Pitṛs", or "to the Pitṛs endowed with Soma".) Why is the number "six potsherds" prescribed? The Pitṛs are themselves of the form of the seasons. The seasons are six in number. Therefore this specification of number.

अथ पितृभ्यो बर्हिषद्भ्यः । अन्वाहार्यपचने धानाः कुर्वंति ततोऽर्धाः पिग्ंषंत्यर्था इत्येव धाना अपिष्टा भवंति ता धानाः पितृभ्यो बर्हिपद्भ्यः ॥ (*atha pitṛbhyo barhiṣadbhyaḥ | anvāhāryapacane dhānāḥ kurvaṃti tato 'rdhāḥ pigṃṣaṃtyarthā ityeva dhānā apiṣṭā bhavaṃti tā dhānāḥ pitṛbhyo barhipadbhyaḥ ‖*) (Śa. Brā. 2-6-1-5)

Afterwards, in the dakṣiṇāgni called Anvāhārya, barley grains are to be parched according to rule. Of these, half is made into flour and the rest is kept as it is. This is the oblation offered to the Pitṛs called Barhiṣads.

### Printed p. 450
अथ पितृभ्योऽग्निष्वात्तेभ्यः । निदान्यायै दुग्धे सकृदुपमथित एकशलाकया मंथो भवति सकृदु ह्येव परांचः पितरस्तस्मात्सकृदुपमथितो भवत्येतानि हवीग्ंषि भवंति ॥ (*atha pitṛbhyo 'gniṣvāttebhyaḥ | nidānyāyai dugdhe sakṛdupamathita ekaśalākayā maṃtho bhavati sakṛdu hyeva parāṃcaḥ pitarastasmātsakṛdupamathito bhavatyetāni havīgṃṣi bhavaṃti ‖*) (Śa. Brā. 2. ?. 1. 6) **NOTE**

Then an oblation, mixed with milk drawn from a cow that lovingly licks her calf and made with wheat flour, is to be offered to the Pitṛs called Agniṣvātta. In this way the manner of the oblations offered at the time of the Mahāpitṛyajña is described. These Pitṛs are classed as Somavantaḥ, Barhiṣadaḥ and Agniṣvāttāḥ. This classification was stated above by citing the sentence तद्ये सोमेनेजानाः (*tadye somenejānāḥ*) (Śa. Brā. 2-6-1-7). In describing the power of this Mahāpitṛyajña, the power of the Pitṛs worshipped here is also extolled greatly. Thus the Pitṛ-śrāddhas are prescribed in many ways. In sum, there is the faith that by the performance of these prescribed śrāddhas and the like the Pitṛs are satisfied, and that thereby good comes to the living. Because it is done with faith (śraddhā), this rite is well known by the name śrāddha.

Only a few sentences praising the Pitṛs, who have the nature of deities, are cited, and this section is for the present brought to a close.

अंगिरोभिरा गहि यज्ञयेभिमैर्यम वैरूपैरिह मादयस्व । विवस्वंतं हुवे यः पिता तेऽस्मिन् यज्ञे बर्हिष्या निषद्य ॥ (*aṃgirobhirā gahi yajñayebhimairyama vairūpairiha mādayasva | vivasvaṃtaṃ huve yaḥ pitā te 'smin yajñe barhiṣyā niṣadya ‖*) (Ṛ. Saṃ. 10-14-5)

O Yama, king, come to this Pitṛ-sacrifice of ours together with the Pitṛs, who assume various forms, are worthy of the highest worship and are called Aṅgirases; I pray that Vivasvat, your father, too, may come to this sacrifice.

मातली कन्यैरमो अंगिरोभिर्बृहस्पतिर्यक्वभिर्वावृधानः । यांश्च देवा वावृधुर्ये च देवान्त्स्वाहाने स्वधयान्ये मदंति ॥ (*mātalī kanyairamo aṃgirobhirbṛhaspatiryakvabhirvāvṛdhānaḥ | yāṃśca devā vāvṛdhurye ca devāntsvāhāne svadhayānye madaṃti ‖*) (Ṛ. Saṃ. 10-14-3)

May Indra, together with Mātali, thrive along with the Pitṛs who partake of kavya. May Yama thrive with the Aṅgirases. May Bṛhaspati thrive with the Ṛkvans. The gods, Indra and the others, whom the Pitṛs cause to thrive, are satisfied with the oblations offered with the cry svāhā. The Pitṛs whom Indra and the other gods cause to thrive are satisfied with the oblations in the form of svadhā.

### Printed p. 451
अग्निस्वात्ताः पितर एह गच्छत सदःसदः सदत सुप्रणीतयः । अत्ता हवींषि प्रयतानि बर्हिष्यथा रयिं सर्ववीरं दधातन ॥ (*agnisvāttāḥ pitara eha gacchata sadaḥsadaḥ sadata supraṇītayaḥ | attā havīṃṣi prayatāni barhiṣyathā rayiṃ sarvavīraṃ dadhātana ‖*) (Ṛ. Saṃ. 10-15-11)

O Pitṛs called Agniṣvātta, come to this Pitṛ-sacrifice of ours. Sit in the places appointed for each of you. Partake of the oblations offered on the sacred grass seat. Provide us all wealth and bring us well-being.

आच्या जानु दक्षिणतो निषद्येमं यज्ञमभि गृणीत विश्वे । मा हिंसिष्ट पितरः केन चिन्नो यद्व आगः पुरुषता कराम ॥ (*ācyā jānu dakṣiṇato niṣadyemaṃ yajñamabhi gṛṇīta viśve | mā hiṃsiṣṭa pitaraḥ kena cinno yadva āgaḥ puruṣatā karāma ‖*) (Ṛ. Saṃ. 10-15-6)

O Pitṛs, sit on the right side, bending your left knees down. Partake of this sacrifice of ours. Do us no harm of any kind. If through the ignorance and weakness natural to human beings we have committed any sinful act, destroy it and forgive us. Grant that all well-being may come to us. Thus the Pitṛs, who have attained divinity, are praised and prayed to.

**Some details in the Ṛks concerning the Pitṛs**

Among the dead, the meritorious dwell in the third heaven; these are called Pitṛs. They are the original ancestors who followed the ancient paths (10-15-8, 10). The dead follow the very path laid down by these seers and go to them (10-14-2, 7, 15). They are connected with the third step of Viṣṇu (10-15-3; compare 1-154-5). Two sūktas have the Pitṛs as deity (10-15; 10-16).

Among the Pitṛs there are the groups Navagvas, Virūpas, Aṅgirases, Atharvans, Bhṛgus and Vasiṣṭhas (10-14-4 to 6; 10-15-8). Of these the last four names are also the names of the seers of the Atharvaveda and of the second and seventh maṇḍalas of the Ṛgveda. Among them the Aṅgirases and Yama have a special connection (10-14-3, 5). Among the Pitṛs there is also a division into avarāḥ (lower rank), parāḥ (higher rank) and madhyamāḥ (middle rank). Even though they are not all known to their descendants, Agni knows all of them (10-15-1, 2, 13). Together with the Uṣases, rivers, mountains, heaven and earth, Pūṣan and the Ṛbhus, the favour of the Pitṛs is also prayed for (6-52-4; 6-75-10; 7-35-12; 1-106-3). Those who seek their regard (10-14-6) pray that wealth, offspring and long life be given to their descendants (10-15-7, 11; Ath. Saṃ. 18-3-14; 18-4-62). **NOTE** The Vasiṣṭhas are prayed to help their descendants (7-33-1; compare 10-15-8);

### Printed p. 452
Śuryaśa (?), Yadu and Ugradeva are praised even individually (1-36-18). **NOTE**

The Pitṛs are also immortal (Ath. Saṃ. 6-41-3); they are even called gods (10-56-4). **NOTE** Among the Aṅgirases and some groups, the status of priest (ṛtvij) is joined to divinity. Acts of creation are also ascribed to some of the Pitṛs: it was they who adorned the sky with stars; day-light and night-darkness came from them (10-68-11); they discovered the hidden light and brought about the dawn (7-26-4; compare 10-107-1); and, joined with Soma, they extended heaven and earth (8-48-13). Just as there is a difference between the Agni that carries the offering to the gods (havyavāha) and the Agni that consumes corpses (kravyāda) (10-16-9), there is also a difference between the path of the gods and the path of the Pitṛs (compare 10-2-7; 10-18-1; 10-88-15). Likewise a distinction between the world of heaven and the world of the Pitṛs is stated; the door of the world of the gods is said to lie in the north-east (Śa. Brā. 6. 6-2-9), and the door of the world of the Pitṛs in the south-east (Śa. Brā. 13. 8. 1-5). The Pitṛs and human beings are of different classes, and their creation is separate (Tai. Brā. 2. 3-8-2). The Pitṛs dwell on earth, in the atmosphere and in heaven (Ath. Saṃ. 18-2. 49; compare Ṛ. Saṃ. 10-152). **NOTE**

The ancient Pitṛs themselves once offered the Soma oblation (10-15-8). They pass their time happily with Yama (10-14-1; compare 10-135-1 and Ath. Saṃ. 18-4-10) and dine with the gods (7-76-4). Living as equals of the gods, they sometimes receive worship fit for the gods. They too come in the chariot of Indra and the gods (10-15-10). They too have a longing for the Soma juice (10-15-5, 6); seated on the sacred grass facing south, they drink the pressed drink (10-15-5, 6). They are eager to drink the Soma juice prepared for them; they are invited to come with Yama, his father Vivasvat and Agni, and with them to accept what has been offered (10-15-8 to 11; 10-14-4, 5). They come in thousands and sit in order on the sacred grass (10-15-10, 11). When the Pitṛs come to the sacrificial hall, certain piśācas also, in the guise of their friends, mingle with them (Ath. Saṃ. 18-2-28).

When food is offered to the gods one says "स्वाहा (*svāhā*)", and when it is given to the Pitṛs "स्वधा (*svadhā*)" (10-15-3); in all rites this difference between the share of the gods and that of the Pitṛs must be kept (Śa. Brā. 4-4-2-2). They too are worshipped; there are prayers that they should hear the prayer of their followers and take their side, and should pardon the lapses that naturally occur (10-15-2, 5, 6; compare 3-55-2).

### Printed p. 453

##### ॥ सायणभाष्यम् ॥ (Sāyaṇa-bhāṣya)

> परेयिवांसमिति षोडशर्चं चतुर्दशं सूक्तं विवस्वतः पुत्रस्य यमस्यार्षं ।
> अंगिरसो नः पितरो नवग्वा इति षष्ठ्या अंगिरःपित्रथर्वभृगुलक्षणा लिंगोक्ता
> देवताः ! प्रेहीत्याद्यास्तिस्रो लिंगोक्तदेवताकाः पितृदेवताका ना । अति द्रव
> सारमेयावित्यादिकस्त्वचः सरमापुत्रौ यौ श्वानौ परलोकर्मार्गमभितः स्थितौ
> तद्देवताकः । शिष्टा यमदेवत्याः । यमाय सोममिति त्रयोदश्याद्या अनुष्टुभः।
> यमाय मधुमत्तममित्येषा बृहती । आदितो द्वादश त्रिष्टुभः । तथा चानुक्रांतं ।
> परेयिवांसं षोळश यमो यामं षष्ठि लिंगोक्तदेवता पराश्च तिस्रः पित्रा वा
> तृचः श्वभ्यां परा अनुष्टुभो बृहत्कुपांत्येति ॥ गतः सूक्तविनियोगः ॥ महापितृयज्ञे यमयागाख्या याज्या । सूत्रितं च । इमं यम प्रस्तरमा हि सीदेति द्वे
> परेयिवांसं प्रवतो महीरनु । आ-२-१९ । इति ॥

##### Gist of the bhāṣya

Sāyaṇa states the seer, deity, metre and use of the sūkta. The sixteen-verse fourteenth sūkta, परेयिवांसं (*pareyivāṃsaṃ*), is the ṛṣi-work of Yama, son of Vivasvat. The sixth verse, अंगिरसो नः पितरो नवग्वा (*aṃgiraso naḥ pitaro navagvā*), has as its deities the Aṅgirases, Pitṛs, Atharvans and Bhṛgus, named in the verse itself. The three verses beginning प्रेहि (*prehi*) (7–9) have as deities those named in the verse, or the Pitṛs. The verses beginning अति द्रव सारमेयौ (*ati drava sārameyau*) (10–12) have as deity the two dogs, sons of Saramā, who stand on the path to the other world. The rest are addressed to Yama. The thirteenth verse, यमाय सोमं (*yamāya somaṃ*), and those following are Anuṣṭubh; यमाय मधुमत्तमं (*yamāya madhumattamaṃ*) is a Bṛhatī; the first twelve are Triṣṭubh. He cites the Anukramaṇī to the same effect. The use of the sūkta has been given. In the Mahāpitṛyajña, in the sacrifice called Yamayāga, the verse serves as yājyā. It is prescribed in the sūtra: इमं यम प्रस्तरमा हि सीदेति द्वे परेयिवांसं प्रवतो महीरनु । (*imaṃ yama prastaramā hi sīdeti dve pareyivāṃsaṃ pravato mahīranu |*) (Ā. 2-19).

##### Anuvāda (Kannada)

This sūkta, परेयिवांसं (*pareyivāṃsaṃ*), is the fourteenth sūkta in the first anuvāka. It has sixteen ṛks. Its seer is Yama, son of Vivasvat. For the sixth verse, अंगिरसो नः (*aṃgiraso naḥ*), the deities are the Pitṛs, named in the verse as Aṅgiras, Pitṛ, Atharvan and Bhṛgu. For the three verses 7–9 beginning प्रेहि (*prehi*) the deities are those named in the verse, or the Pitṛs. For verses 10–12, अति द्रव सारमेयौ (*ati drava sārameyau*), the deities are the two dogs, the Sārameyas, sons of the divine bitch Saramā who is on the path of the other world. The remaining verses are addressed to Yama. The four verses from यमाय सोमं (*yamāya somaṃ*) (13–16) are in Anuṣṭubh metre; the fifteenth, यमाय मधुमत्तमं (*yamāya madhumattamaṃ*), is in Bṛhatī. The first twelve verses are in Triṣṭubh. In the Anukramaṇī it is said: परेयिवांसं षोळश यमो यामं षष्ठि लिंगोक्तदेवता पराश्चतिस्रः पित्रा वा तृचः श्वभ्यां परा अनुष्टुभो बृहत्युपांत्या (*pareyivāṃsaṃ ṣoḷaśa yamo yāmaṃ ṣaṣṭhi liṃgoktadevatā parāścatisraḥ pitrā vā tṛcaḥ śvabhyāṃ parā anuṣṭubho bṛhatyupāṃtyā*). The use of the sūkta was stated earlier. In the Yamayāga of the rite called Mahāpitṛyajña, the first ṛk of the sūkta is to be recited as yājyā mantra, as laid down in the Āśvalāyana Śrauta Sūtra: इमं यम प्रस्तरमा हि सीदेति द्वे परेयिवांसं प्रवतो महीरनु (*imaṃ yama prastaramā hi sīdeti dve pareyivāṃsaṃ pravato mahīranu*) (Ā. 2-19).

##### Particulars

Sūkta 14
Maṇḍala 10; Anuvāka 1; Sūkta 14.
Aṣṭaka 7; Adhyāya 6; Vargas 14, 15, 16.
Number of ṛks in the sūkta: 16.
Ṛṣi: Yama.
Deity: 1–5, 13–16 Yama; 6 deities named in the verse; 7–9 deities named in the verse, or the Pitṛs; 10–12 the two dogs.
Metre: 1–12 Triṣṭubh; 13, 14, 16 Anuṣṭubh; 15 Bṛhatī.

##### ॥ संहितापाठः ॥ (Saṃhitā-pāṭha)
