##### भावार्थ (Bhāvārtha)

O Soma, your juice which goes out of the pressing hide and flows, your thing in the form of a plant or the like which goes out from the arm of the adhvaryu, which goes out from the boards of pressing, which is offered by the adhvaryu, or which goes out from the daśā-pavitra and flows: such juice of yours I offer in the form of an oblation, with praise and with the vaṣaṭ-call.

##### English translation
Your juice, (Soma), which escapes (from the hide), your filaments which let fall from the hands (of the priest escape) from the vicinity of the planks (of the press), or (from the hand) of the Adhwaryu, or from the filter; I offer it all with my mind (to Agni) with the word vashat.

##### विशेषविषयगळु (Special Topics)

Here it is necessary to explain in detail what the vaṣaṭkāra is, why it is to be recited, what its nature and sign are, and so on. When oblations are to be offered in sacrifices to the various deities, since those deities are not visible to us, mantras addressed to each deity are recited with that deity in view and the offering is made in the fire. In making the offering in that way, they add the word svāhā or नौषट् (*nauṣaṭ*)**NOTE** at the end of the mantra and recite it while offering. Before making the offering, certain rules have to be followed. First the deity to whom the oblation is to be offered is described in his qualities with mantras of praise and the like addressed to that deity. These mantras describing qualities are called śastra mantras and nivit mantras. Since in the nivid mantra the special qualities of that deity are described, the nivid mantra is inserted in the middle of the śastra mantras and recited. After the qualities have been described in this way, the priest called hotṛ invites the deity with another mantra to come to the sacrificial ground. This inviting mantra is called anuvākyā or puronuvākyā mantra. Then, imagining that the deity has accepted the invitation, come to the sacrificial ground and seated himself on the seat of darbha grass called barhis,

### Printed p. 568
the priest called adhvaryu offers the oblation in the fire with yet another mantra. This mantra, at the time of offering, is called yājyā. At the very end of this yājyā mantra they add the word svāhā or vauṣaṭ and make the offering. To make this clear we shall give an example. At the occasion when the offering is to be made to Viṣṇu himself, the priest called Acchāvāka recites for the śastra mantras the sūkta addressed to Viṣṇu, नू मर्तो दयते (*nū marto dayate*) (the hundredth sūkta of the 7th Maṇḍala). In the middle of these mantras he inserts and recites as nivid mantras some mantras that sing the qualities of Viṣṇu, that is, the three ṛks beginning प्र तत्ते अद्य (*pra tatte adya*) (Ṛ. Saṃ. 7-100-5 to 6-100-7)**NOTE**. Then, to invite Viṣṇu,

न ते विष्णो जायमानो न जातो देव महिम्नः परमंतमाप उदस्तभ्ना नाकमृष्टं बृहंतं दादर्थ प्राचीं ककुभं पृथिव्याः ॥ (*na te viṣṇo jāyamāno na jāto deva mahimnaḥ paramaṃtamāpa udastabhnā nākamṛṣṭaṃ bṛhaṃtaṃ dādartha prācīṃ kakubhaṃ pṛthivyāḥ ‖*) (Ṛ. Saṃ. 7-99-2)

this ṛk is recited in the animal offering as the anuvākyā mantra, and the hotṛ invites the deity Viṣṇu. Then,

त्रिर्देवः पृथिवीमेष एतां वि चक्रमे शतर्चसं महित्वा । प्र विष्णुरस्तु तवसस्तवीयान्वेषं ह्यस्य स्थविरस्य नाम ॥ (*trirdevaḥ pṛthivīmeṣa etāṃ vi cakrame śatarcasaṃ mahitvā | pra viṣṇurastu tavasastavīyānveṣaṃ hyasya sthavirasya nāma ‖*) (Ṛ. Saṃ. 7-100-3)

this ṛk he recites as the yājyā mantra. After the words स्थविरस्य नाम (*sthavirasya nāma*) at the end of this mantra he adds the word वौषट् (*vauṣaṭ*), reciting स्थविरस्य नाम वौषट् (*sthavirasya nāma vauṣaṭ*), and offers in the fire the part of the animal called vasā. This order is to be followed also when offering to each deity. But the mantras differ for each deity. Besides, the offering-substance is of many kinds: ājya, havis, puroḍāśa, vapā and so on, and the mantras differ accordingly. The mantras in the example given above are connected only with the vapā offering. In the same way there are separate mantras for the puroḍāśa offering and for the havis offering. And different mantras are to be used in different sacrifices.

Now, what are the nature and sign of the vaṣaṭkāra? Why is it to be used at the end of a mantra? This matter has to be examined. On this point the detailed account given in the Aitareya Brāhmaṇa is set out here:

देवपात्रं वा एतद्यद्वषट्कारो वषट्कारेति देवपात्रॆणैव तद्देवतास्तर्पयति ॥ (*devapātraṃ vā etadyadvaṣaṭkāro vaṣaṭkāreti devapātrèṇaiva taddevatāstarpayati ‖*) (Ai. Bā. 11-5)**NOTE**

### Printed p. 569

Now the nature of the vaṣaṭkāra and the anuvaṣaṭkāra will be explained. The word "वौषट् (*vauṣaṭ*)" recited at the end of a mantra while offering an oblation is called the vaṣaṭkāra. When a food-offering is presented to the gods to be eaten, it must be placed in a vessel or plate, as is customary in ordinary life. Offering it in a vessel makes it easy to eat. In a sacrifice the gods are invisible when they eat the offering. The oblation is offered to the gods by pouring it into Agni, that is, Agni carries to the gods the oblation poured into him for them. But how can the vessel holding the oblation be set before the gods while the oblation is being poured? This is impossible. So the mantra itself is recited in place of the vessel, and it is regarded as the vessel. The mere word "वौषट् (*vauṣaṭ*)" is this vessel. If "वौषट् (*vauṣaṭ*)" is pronounced at the end of the mantra, it is as if the oblation offered with the mantra had been placed in a vessel so that it can be eaten easily. The word "वौषट् (*vauṣaṭ*)" is therefore the vessel that serves the gods for drinking. For this reason, that is, in order to satisfy the gods by offering the oblation to them in a vessel, the hotṛ adds the word "वौषट् (*vauṣaṭ*)" at the end of the mantra, recites it and pours the oblation. This is the meaning of the word vaṣaṭkāra. Next the meaning of anuvaṣaṭkāra is explained:

अनुवषट्करोति तद्यथादोऽश्वान्वा गा वा पुनरभ्याकारं तर्पयंत्येवमेवैतद्देवताः पुनरभ्याकारं तर्पयंति यदनुवषट्करोति............॥ (*anuvaṣaṭkaroti tadyathādo 'śvānvā gā vā punarabhyākāraṃ tarpayaṃtyevamevaitaddevatāḥ punarabhyākāraṃ tarpayaṃti yadanuvaṣaṭkaroti............‖*) (Ai. Brā. 11-5)

In ordinary life people set grass and other fodder before horses, cows and other animals so that they eat, and coax them with endearing words. In the same way, since the oblation has to be offered to the gods through Agni, the Ṛk

अग्ने वीहि पुरोळाशमाहुतं तिरोअह्न्यं । सहसः सूनुरस्यध्वरे हितः ॥ (*agne vīhi puroḷāśamāhutaṃ tiroahnyaṃ | sahasaḥ sūnurasyadhvare hitaḥ ‖*) (Ṛ. Saṃ. 3-28-3)

or else

अग्ने वीहि हविषा यक्षि देवान्तस्यध्वरा कृणुहि जातवेदः । (*agne vīhi haviṣā yakṣi devāntasyadhvarā kṛṇuhi jātavedaḥ |*) (Ṛ. Saṃ. 3-17-3)

must be recited. Its meaning: "O Agni, eat this oblation or this purodāśa, or drink this soma juice. Convey to the gods this oblation offered into you through the homa." This Ṛk is to be recited to please the gods. It is called the anuvaṣaṭkāra.

### Printed p. 570

वज्रो वा एष यद्वषट्कारो यं द्विष्यात्तं ध्यायेद्वषट्करिष्यंस्तस्मिन्नेव तं वज्रमास्थापयति । (*vajro vā eṣa yadvaṣaṭkāro yaṃ dviṣyāttaṃ dhyāyedvaṣaṭkariṣyaṃstasminneva taṃ vajramāsthāpayati |*) (Ai. Brā. 11-6)

The vaṣaṭkāra is a powerful weapon like the thunderbolt. If the sacrificer has an enemy and wishes to destroy him, then while offering the oblation with this vaṣaṭkāra he should pour the homa meditating in his mind "may that enemy be destroyed"; the vaṣaṭkāra then strikes that enemy like the blow of a thunderbolt and kills him.

षळिति वषट्करोति षड्वा ऋतवः ऋतूनेव तत्कल्पयत्यतून्प्रतिष्ठापयत्यतून्वै प्रतितिष्ठत इदं सर्वमनु प्रतितिष्ठति यदितं किंच ॥ (*ṣaḷiti vaṣaṭkaroti ṣaḍvā ṛtavaḥ ṛtūneva tatkalpayatyatūnpratiṣṭhāpayatyatūnvai pratitiṣṭhata idaṃ sarvamanu pratitiṣṭhati yaditaṃ kiṃca ‖*)

The word "वौषट् (*vauṣaṭ*)" contains the word "षट् (*ṣaṭ*)". Here "षट् (*ṣaṭ*)" means the six seasons. There are six seasons in a year. So if one offers the oblation with the vaṣaṭkāra, he satisfies the six seasons. Not only that: since everything is thereby satisfied, he becomes victorious in all undertakings. The next passage explains this at length:

प्रतितिष्ठति य एवं वेद तदु ह स्माह हिरण्यदन्बैद एतानि वा एतेन षट् प्रतिष्ठापयति द्यौरंतरिक्षे प्रतिष्ठितान्तरीक्षं पृथिव्यां पृथिव्यप्स्वापः सत्ये सत्यं ब्रह्मणि ब्रह्म तपसीत्येता एव तत्पतिष्ठांतीरिदं सर्वमनु प्रतितिष्ठति यदिदं किंच प्रतितिष्ठति य एवं वेद........॥ (*pratitiṣṭhati ya evaṃ veda tadu ha smāha hiraṇyadanbaida etāni vā etena ṣaṭ pratiṣṭhāpayati dyauraṃtarikṣe pratiṣṭhitāntarīkṣaṃ pṛthivyāṃ pṛthivyapsvāpaḥ satye satyaṃ brahmaṇi brahma tapasītyetā eva tatpatiṣṭhāṃtīridaṃ sarvamanu pratitiṣṭhati yadidaṃ kiṃca pratitiṣṭhati ya evaṃ veda........‖*) (Ai. Brā. 11-6)

The son of the sage Bidā, whose row of teeth was golden, said this on the subject: by the vaṣaṭkāra the hotṛ, as it were, establishes six places, from the heavenly world up to Brahma. That is: since the atmosphere lies below heaven, heaven rests upon the atmosphere. Likewise the atmosphere rests on the earth, the earth on the waters beneath, and the water on truth. If people are truthful, rain can fall in due season; therefore it is said that water is established in truth. That truth is established in Brahma (the Veda), and Brahma in austerity (tapas), which is the vaṣaṭkāra mantra. Hence it should be understood that the whole world is established in the vaṣaṭkāra. The man who knows this has, as it were, conquered everything.

There are three varieties of vaṣaṭkāra. Their nature is explained:

त्रयो वै वषट्कारा वज्रो धामच्छद्रिक्तः । (*trayo vai vaṣaṭkārā vajro dhāmacchadriktaḥ |*) (Ai. Brā. 11-7)

### Printed p. 571

Among vaṣaṭkāras there are three kinds: vajra, dhāmacchad and rikta.

स यमेवोच्चैर्बलि वषट्करोति स वज्रः । तं तं प्रहरति द्विषते भ्रातृव्याय वधं योऽस्य स्तृत्यस्तस्मै स्तरवे तस्मात्स भ्रातृव्यवता वषट्कृत्यः ॥ (*sa yamevoccairbali vaṣaṭkaroti sa vajraḥ | taṃ taṃ praharati dviṣate bhrātṛvyāya vadhaṃ yo 'sya stṛtyastasmai starave tasmātsa bhrātṛvyavatā vaṣaṭkṛtyaḥ ‖*)

Because the hotṛ pronounces this vaṣaṭkāra in a strong voice, it has the name vajra. When the sacrificer wishes to destroy those who are his enemies, then by employing this vaṣaṭkāra it strikes the sacrificer's enemy in the form of a thunderbolt and destroys him. Therefore a sacrificer who desires the destruction of an enemy should use this vaṣaṭkāra in the form of the vajra.

अथ यः समः संततोऽनिर्हाणर्चः स धामच्छत् । तं तं प्रजाश्च पशवश्चानूपतिष्ठंते तस्मात्स प्रजाकामेन पशुकामेन वषट्कृत्यः ॥ (*atha yaḥ samaḥ saṃtato 'nirhāṇarcaḥ sa dhāmacchat | taṃ taṃ prajāśca paśavaścānūpatiṣṭhaṃte tasmātsa prajākāmena paśukāmena vaṣaṭkṛtyaḥ ‖*)

Here an explanation of the manner of pronouncing the vaṣaṭkāra is needed. It was stated earlier that the word "वौषट् (*vauṣaṭ*)" is to be added and recited at the end of the yājyā mantra. In this connection, "वौषट् (*vauṣaṭ*)" must be pronounced in three ways, according to the three kinds of vaṣaṭkāra: vajra, dhāmacchad and rikta. When the vaṣaṭkāra called vajra is used, the yājyā mantra is pronounced in an ordinary voice, and at the end "वौषट् (*vauṣaṭ*)" is pronounced in a strong voice; and the last syllable of the yājyā mantra is joined with the syllable Om, that is, the last syllable is pronounced as if combined with Om, and then "वौषट् (*vauṣaṭ*)" is pronounced in a strong voice. In the Ṛk given earlier as an example,

त्रिर्देवः पृथिवीमेष एतां वि चक्रमे शतर्चसं महित्वा । प्र विष्णुरस्तु तवसस्तवीयान्वेषं ह्यस्य स्थविरस्य नाम ॥ (*trirdevaḥ pṛthivīmeṣa etāṃ vi cakrame śatarcasaṃ mahitvā | pra viṣṇurastu tavasastavīyānveṣaṃ hyasya sthavirasya nāma ‖*)

the last part is "स्थविरस्य नाम (*sthavirasya nāma*)". If Om is added to it, it becomes स्थविरस्य नामों (*sthavirasya nāmoṃ*). The Ṛk is thus pronounced स्थविरस्य नामों (*sthavirasya nāmoṃ*) in an even voice, and then the word "वौषट् (*vauṣaṭ*)" is pronounced in a strong voice. This is the manner of pronouncing the vaṣaṭkāra called vajra. Now, to pronounce the vaṣaṭkāra called dhāmacchad, the yājyā mantra is pronounced without any alteration, that is, only as स्थविरस्य नाम (*sthavirasya nāma*) (without Om at the end), and then the word "वौषट् (*vauṣaṭ*)" is recited. This is the manner of pronouncing the vaṣaṭkāra called dhāmacchad. The sacrificer who desires offspring and cattle should pour the homa with this dhāmacchad kind of vaṣaṭkāra.

### Printed p. 572

अथ येनैव षळवराध्नोति स रिक्तः । रिणक्त्यात्मानं रिणक्ति यजमानं पापीयान्षट्कर्ता भवति पापीयान्यस्मै वषट्करोति तस्मात्तस्याशां नेयात् ॥ (*atha yenaiva ṣaḷavarādhnoti sa riktaḥ | riṇaktyātmānaṃ riṇakti yajamānaṃ pāpīyānṣaṭkartā bhavati pāpīyānyasmai vaṣaṭkaroti tasmāttasyāśāṃ neyāt ‖*)

If, in pronouncing the word "वौषट् (*vauṣaṭ*)", the syllable "षट् (*ṣaṭ*)" is pronounced softly in a low voice, that vaṣaṭkāra is called rikta. Rikta means "empty". So if the homa is poured with this rikta vaṣaṭkāra, the sacrificer is left in an empty state with nothing, and sin also befalls him. The ṛtvij who has the homa performed also becomes the worse sinner. Therefore neither a sacrificer nor a ṛtvij who desires welfare should ever use this rikta vaṣaṭkāra.

किं स यजमानस्य पापभद्रमाद्रियेतेति ह स्माह योऽस्य होता स्यादित्यत्रैवैनं यथा कामयेत तथा कुर्यात् । यं कामयेत यथैवानीजानोऽभूत्तथैवेजानः स्यादिति यथैवास्य ऋचं ब्रूयात्तथैवास्य वषट्कुर्यात्सदृशमेवैनं तत्करोति ॥ (*kiṃ sa yajamānasya pāpabhadramādriyeteti ha smāha yo 'sya hotā syādityatraivainaṃ yathā kāmayeta tathā kuryāt | yaṃ kāmayeta yathaivānījāno 'bhūttathaivejānaḥ syāditi yathaivāsya ṛcaṃ brūyāttathaivāsya vaṣaṭkuryātsadṛśamevainaṃ tatkaroti ‖*)

The ṛtvij called hotṛ, who plays the chief part in the sacrifice, may do to the sacrificer whatever he wishes, whether good or ill, as he pleases. For example, if the hotṛ wishes that the sacrificer should not obtain the proper fruit of the sacrifice, then, instead of pronouncing the yājyā mantra in the ordinary manner and the vaṣaṭkāra strongly, the hotṛ pronounces the yājyā and the vaṣaṭkāra mantras in one even voice; the sacrificer then does not obtain the fruit of the sacrifice.

यं कामयेत पापीयान्स्यादित्युच्चैस्तरामस्य ऋचमुक्त्वा शनैस्तरां वषट्कुर्यात्पापीयांसमेवैनं तत्करोति (*yaṃ kāmayeta pāpīyānsyādityuccaistarāmasya ṛcamuktvā śanaistarāṃ vaṣaṭkuryātpāpīyāṃsamevainaṃ tatkaroti*)

If the hotṛ wishes that the sacrificer should not obtain the fruit of the sacrifice and that only sin should befall him, then he should recite the Ṛk of the yājyā mantra in a strong voice and the vaṣaṭkāra in a soft voice. If he does so, sin befalls the sacrificer.

यं कामयेत श्रेयान्सादिति शनैस्तरामस्य ऋचमुक्तोच्चैंस्तरां वषट्कुर्याच्छ्रिय एवैनं तच्छ्रियमादधाति । (*yaṃ kāmayeta śreyānsāditi śanaistarāmasya ṛcamuktoccaiṃstarāṃ vaṣaṭkuryācchriya evainaṃ tacchriyamādadhāti |*)

Otherwise, if the hotṛ wishes that welfare should come to the sacrificer, then the yājyā mantra should be pronounced in a soft voice and the vaṣaṭkāra in a strong voice. If he does so, welfare comes to the sacrificer.

संततमृचा वषट्कश्यं संतत्यै । संधीयते प्रजया पशुभिर्य एवं वेद ॥ (*saṃtatamṛcā vaṣaṭkaśyaṃ saṃtatyai | saṃdhīyate prajayā paśubhirya evaṃ veda ‖*) (Ai. Brā. 11-7)

### Printed p. 573

One important matter must be observed in pronouncing the yājyā mantra and the vaṣaṭkāra. After the yājyā mantra has been pronounced to its end, the vaṣaṭkāra must not be pronounced after a short pause. Regarding the vaṣaṭkāra as one (final) part of the yājyā mantra, one should pronounce it continuously, in an unbroken flow, from the beginning of the Ṛk up to "वौषट् (*vauṣaṭ*)", without stopping anywhere in between. The man who knows this obtains offspring and wealth in cattle and lives happily.

There are certain rules that the hotṛ must follow in reciting the vaṣaṭkāra. They must be observed without fail. Otherwise, just as danger arises from using a sharp weapon, harm arises from using the vaṣaṭkāra:

यस्यै देवताय्कॆ हविर्गृहीतं स्यात्तां ध्यायेद्वषट्करिष्यन्साक्षादेव तद्देवतां प्रिणाति प्रत्यक्षाद्देवतां यजति । (*yasyai devatāykè havirgṛhītaṃ syāttāṃ dhyāyedvaṣaṭkariṣyansākṣādeva taddevatāṃ priṇāti pratyakṣāddevatāṃ yajati |*) (the reference is printed as प (*pa*). बस- ११ (*basa- 11*).८ (*8*)) **NOTE**

The hotṛ should meditate in his mind on the deity for whom he pours the homa with the vaṣaṭkāra, pronounce the mantra and pour the homa with the vaṣaṭkāra. If he does so, it is as if he had made the deity visible and satisfied her. Is it possible to see the gods directly, that is, to perceive them? Seeing them directly with the eyes is not possible. But by meditating in the mind one can imagine that the deity stands visible before one. This itself may be called "direct".

वज्रो वै वषट्कारः स एष प्रहृतोशांतो दीदाय तस्य हैतस्य न सर्व इव शांतिं वेद न प्रतिष्ठां तस्माद्दाप्येतर्हि भूयानिव मृत्युस्तस्य हैषैव शांतिरेषा प्रतिष्ठा वागित्येव तस्याद्वषट्कृत्य वागित्यनुमंत्रयेत स एनं शांतो न हिनस्ति ॥ (*vajro vai vaṣaṭkāraḥ sa eṣa prahṛtośāṃto dīdāya tasya haitasya na sarva iva śāṃtiṃ veda na pratiṣṭhāṃ tasmāddāpyetarhi bhūyāniva mṛtyustasya haiṣaiva śāṃtireṣā pratiṣṭhā vāgityeva tasyādvaṣaṭkṛtya vāgityanumaṃtrayeta sa enaṃ śāṃto na hinasti ‖*)

It was said earlier that the vaṣaṭkāra is sharp like a thunderbolt and that harm results if it is not used properly. Not everyone knows how to use it. Just as many meet death in wars when weapons are used heedlessly without knowing the method, so here too many may suffer harm from the misuse of the vaṣaṭkāra mantra. Therefore, to pacify it, the mantra beginning वागोजः (*vāgojaḥ*) should be recited. By reciting this mantra the harm that might arise from misuse of the vaṣaṭkāra is removed. There is no other remedy for such harm. So at the time of the sacrifice the mantra वागोजः (*vāgojaḥ*) should be recited after every vaṣaṭkāra. If this is done, no evil comes from the vaṣaṭkāra, which is of the nature of the thunderbolt. This is the view of some. Others speak differently.

### Printed p. 574

वषट्कार मा मां प्रमृक्षो माहं त्वां प्रमृक्षं बृहता मन उपह्वये व्यानेन शरीरं प्रतिष्ठासि प्रतिष्ठां गच्छ प्रतिष्ठां मा गमयेति वषट्कारमनुमंत्रयेत ॥ (*vaṣaṭkāra mā māṃ pramṛkṣo māhaṃ tvāṃ pramṛkṣaṃ bṛhatā mana upahvaye vyānena śarīraṃ pratiṣṭhāsi pratiṣṭhāṃ gaccha pratiṣṭhāṃ mā gamayeti vaṣaṭkāramanumaṃtrayeta ‖*)

Concerning the anumantraṇa (pacification), the sacrificer should say as follows: "O vaṣaṭkāra, do not thrust me, who am performing the sacrifice, aside and destroy me; I too shall not thrust you away. By this great sacrificial rite I win over your mind. With the vyāna and the other winds I pervade your body and cooperate with you. You are the support of the whole multitude of living beings. Therefore go to your own excellent place, and grant that I too may go to mine." So the sacrificer should pray.

तदु ह स्माह दीर्घमेतत्सदप्रभ्वोजः सह ओजः । इत्येव वषट्कारमनुमंत्रयेत । ओजश्च ह वै सहश्च वषट्कारस्य प्रियतमे तन्वौ प्रियेणैवैनं तद्धाम्ना समर्धयति प्रियेण धाम्ना समृध्यते य एवं वेद ॥ (*tadu ha smāha dīrghametatsadaprabhvojaḥ saha ojaḥ | ityeva vaṣaṭkāramanumaṃtrayeta | ojaśca ha vai sahaśca vaṣaṭkārasya priyatame tanvau priyeṇaivainaṃ taddhāmnā samardhayati priyeṇa dhāmnā samṛdhyate ya evaṃ veda ‖*)

Some Brahmavādins say: this mantra is very long, so reciting it is very laborious; moreover, does it pacify the vaṣaṭkāra, which is of the nature of the thunderbolt, or not? Therefore the short mantra ओजः सह ओज; (*ojaḥ saha oja;*), which pacifies the vaṣaṭkāra, may be recited. This mantra has only three words. Ojas means capacity, sahas means strength; these two are said to be the dear bodies of the vaṣaṭkāra. By thus pronouncing the bodies dear to the vaṣaṭkāra, the anger and the like that arise in the vaṣaṭkāra from deficiency in the mantra and so on are pacified, and it brings benefit to the sacrificer. The third word of the mantra, ओजः (*ojaḥ*), is repeated out of respect; it has no separate meaning. To the man who knows this the vaṣaṭkāra brings prosperity.

वाच्य वै प्राणापानौ च वषट्कारस्त एते वषट्कृते वषट्कृते व्यत्क्रामंति ताननुमंत्रयेत नागोजः सह ओजो मयि प्राणापानावित्यात्मन्येव तद्धोता वाचं च प्राणापानौ च प्रतिष्ठापयति सर्वायुः सर्वायुत्वाय सर्वमायुरेति य एवं वेद ॥ (*vācya vai prāṇāpānau ca vaṣaṭkārasta ete vaṣaṭkṛte vaṣaṭkṛte vyatkrāmaṃti tānanumaṃtrayeta nāgojaḥ saha ojo mayi prāṇāpānāvityātmanyeva taddhotā vācaṃ ca prāṇāpānau ca pratiṣṭhāpayati sarvāyuḥ sarvāyutvāya sarvamāyureti ya evaṃ veda ‖*) (Ai. Brā. 11-8)

Speech, prāṇa (in-breath) and apāna (out-breath) are the nature of the vaṣaṭkāra. Whenever the hotṛ pronounces the vaṣaṭkāra at the end of a mantra, this speech, prāṇa and apāna go out of the hotṛ's body. To prevent this, they must be included in the anumantraṇa. वागोजः सह ओजो मयि प्राणापानौ (*vāgojaḥ saha ojo mayi prāṇāpānau*) is that anumantraṇa. Its meaning: capacity

### Printed p. 575
...the sense continues: the power and strength, the two dear bodily (companions). O Vaṣaṭkāra, by your grace may power and strength abide in me. And may speech, the in-breath and the out-breath also not depart from my body but stay firmly in me. By reciting this mantra, which has this meaning, the Hotṛ becomes able to prevent speech, the in-breath and the out-breath from going out, and to keep them in himself. Because of this he obtains his appointed full span of life (a hundred years). The man who knows this matter also obtains the full span of life and is happy.

#### Ṛk 13

##### ॥ संहितापाठः ॥ (Saṃhitā-pāṭha)

> यस्ते॑ द्र॒प्सः स्क॒न्नो यस्थे॑ अं॒शुर॒वश्च॒ यः प॒रः स्रु॒चा ॥  
> अ॒यं दे॒वो बृह॒स्पतिः॒ सं तं सिं॑चतु॒ राध॑से ॥ १३ ॥

##### ॥ पदपाठः ॥ (Pada-pāṭha)

> यः । ते । द्रप्सः । स्कन्नः । यः । ते । अंशुः । अवः । च । यः । परः । स्रुचा ।  
> अयं । देवः । बृहस्पतिः । सं । तं । सिंचतु । राधसे ॥ १३ ॥

##### ॥ सायणभाष्यम् ॥ (Sāyaṇa-bhāṣya)

> हे सोम ते त्वदीयो यो द्रप्पो रसोऽन्यत्र स्कन्नो गतो यश्च
> त्वदीयस्तव कारणभूतोऽंशुर्लताखंडो रसादितरो भवति स्पुचा पात्रविशेषेण
> गृहीतः सोमोऽवोऽवस्तात्स्कंदते परः परस्ताद्वातिरिक्तो भवति तमिमं
> सोममयं बृहस्पतिरेतन्नामको देवः सं सिंचतु । सम्यक् प्रक्षारयतु ।
> किमर्थं । राधसेऽस्माकं धनार्थं । स्कन्ने हि सोमे प्रजापश्वादिकमपस्कन्नं
> भवति खलु ॥

##### Gist of the bhāṣya

Sāyaṇa addresses Soma: "O Soma, your juice (द्रप्सः (*drapsaḥ*)) that has dropped elsewhere, and your filament (अंशुः (*aṃśuḥ*)), the piece of the plant that is the source of the juice, which, held in the ladle (स्रुचा (*srucā*), a particular vessel), falls below, or is otherwise left over or beyond — that Soma may this god named Bṛhaspati sprinkle thoroughly, that is, cause to flow properly." For what purpose? "For राधसे (*rādhase*), for our wealth." For when Soma is spilt, offspring, cattle and the like are indeed spilt as well.

##### प्रतिपदार्थ (Pratipadārtha)

- ते (*te*)—your
- यः द्रप्सः (*yaḥ drapsaḥ*)—which juice
- स्कन्नः (*skannaḥ*)—flows out
- यः ते अंशुः (*yaḥ te aṃśuḥ*)—which plant
- स्रुचा (*srucā*)—held by the ladle
- अवः (*avaḥ*)—to the lower part
- यः परः च (*yaḥ paraḥ ca*)—and which is spilt to the other parts
- तं (*taṃ*)—that juice-filled Soma
- देवः अयं बृहस्पतिः (*devaḥ ayaṃ bṛhaspatiḥ*)—this god Bṛhaspati
- राधसे (*rādhase*)—for the gaining of wealth for us
- सं सिंचतु (*saṃ siṃcatu*)—may he sprinkle all around

### Printed p. 576

##### भावार्थ (Bhāvārtha)

O Soma, the juice of yours that flows out, and the plant held by the ladle that is spilt below and to other parts — that juice-filled Soma, may this god Bṛhaspati sprinkle all around (offer) for the gaining of wealth for us.

##### English translation
Your juice and your filaments, (Soma), which escape, and which fall from the ladle on this side or on that; may this divine Brihaspati sprinkle it for our enrichment.

#### Ṛk 14

##### ॥ संहितापाठः ॥ (Saṃhitā-pāṭha)

> पय॑स्वती॒रोष॑धयः॒ पय॑स्वन्माम॒कं वचः॑ ।  
> अ॒पां पय॑स्व॒दित्पय॒स्तेन॑ मा स॒ह शुं॑धत ॥ १४ ॥

##### ॥ पदपाठः ॥ (Pada-pāṭha)

> पयस्वतीः । ओषदयः । पयस्वत् । मामकं । वचः ।  
> अपां : पयस्वत् । इत् । पयः । तेन । मा । सह । शुंधत । १४ ॥

##### ॥ सायणभाष्यम् ॥ (Sāyaṇa-bhāṣya)

> इयं प्रत्यक्षकृता । हे आपः ओषधयः पयस्वतीः पयस्वत्यो वृष्टिलक्षणेनोदकेन सारवत्यो भवंति ! मामकं मदीयं वचो वचनं वृष्टिप्रार्थनवचनं पयस्वत्सारवद्भवति ! किं बहुना । यच्चेह किंचिदपामुदकानां पयः
> क्षीरवत्सारभूतं यदस्ति तत्सर्वं पयस्वत्सारवदेव ! तेनोदकसारेण सह मा
> मां शुंधत । यूयं शोधयत । आपो अद्यान्वहारिषं रसेन समगस्महि ।
> ऋ. सं. १.२३.२३ । इति निगमांतरं ॥

##### Gist of the bhāṣya

This Ṛk is addressed directly. "O Waters, the plants become पयस्वतीः (*payasvatīḥ*), full of sap through water in the form of rain. My speech, the prayer for rain, becomes full of substance. Why say more? Whatever essence, like milk, there is here of the waters, all that is full of sap. With that essence of water purify me; you purify." Another Vedic passage is cited: आपो अद्यान्वहारिषं रसेन समगस्महि । (*āpo adyānvahāriṣaṃ rasena samagasmahi |*) (Ṛ. Saṃ. 1.23.23).

##### प्रतिपदार्थ (Pratipadārtha)

- ओषधयः (*oṣadhayaḥ*)—the plants
- पयस्वतीः (*payasvatīḥ*)—become full of substance through the waters
- मामकं (*māmakaṃ*)—my
- वचः (*vacaḥ*)—prayer for rain
- पयस्वत् (*payasvat*)—becomes full of substance
- अपां (*apāṃ*)—of the waters
- पयः पयस्वत् (*payaḥ payasvat*)—all the juice becomes full of substance
- तेन सह (*tena saha*)—with that water-essence
- मा (*mā*)—me
- शुंधत (*śuṃdhata*)—make pure

### Printed p. 577

##### भावार्थ (Bhāvārtha)

O Waters (the Kannada reads "O non-dual ones"), the plants become full of substance through the waters. My prayer for rain becomes full of substance. All the essences of the waters are rich in substance. With that essence of water make me pure. **NOTE**

##### English translation
(Waters)! the plants flourish by means of water, my prayer is effectual through water; the essence of water is vigorous through water; purify me with it.

## Sūkta 18 (Maṇḍala 10)
**Introduction**
In this sūkta are spoken a praise of the deity Death and mantras used in rites for the ancestors. In the Bṛhaddevatā, a work attributed to Śaunaka, it is said of this sūkta:
चतस्रस्ता स्तुतिर्मृत्योरंत्ये क्लप्ताश्च कर्मणि । १० ॥ मृतशिष्टेभ्य आशास्ते इमे ज्योज्जीवनं पुनः । इमं जीवेभ्य आशास्ते तेभ्यः परिधिकर्मणि ॥ (*catasrastā stutirmṛtyoraṃtye klaptāśca karmaṇi | 10 ‖ mṛtaśiṣṭebhya āśāste ime jyojjīvanaṃ punaḥ | imaṃ jīvebhya āśāste tebhyaḥ paridhikarmaṇi ‖*) (10–11)
The first four Ṛks of this sūkta praise the deity Death. These mantras are used in the final rites. In the third Ṛk, इमे जीवा (*ime jīvā*), the wish for long life is expressed for those belonging to the household of the dead and for those still living. The fourth Ṛk, इमं जीवेभ्यः (*imaṃ jīvebhyaḥ*), is applied in the rite of setting a stone around the living, in order to escape death.
यथा धात्र्युत्तरा त्वाष्ट्री ततो यान्या इमास्ति । स्त्रीणामाशिषमाशास्ते तय्यैवांजनकर्मणि ॥ (*yathā dhātryuttarā tvāṣṭrī tato yānyā imāsti | strīṇāmāśiṣamāśāste tayyaivāṃjanakarmaṇi ‖*) (12)
The Ṛks 5, 6 and 7 of this sūkta, यथाहानि (*yathāhāni*), आरोहत (*ārohata*) and इमा नारीः (*imā nārīḥ*), are to be recited when the women belonging to the household of the dead smear their eyes with ghee or collyrium (black); in these Ṛks the assurance of long life for those women is expressed. Of these, Dhātṛ is the deity of the 5th Ṛk and Tvaṣṭṛ of the 6th.

### Printed p. 578
उद्दीर्ष्वनारीत्यनया मृतं पत्न्यनुरोहति । भ्राता कनीयान्प्रेतस्य निगद्य प्रतिषेधति ॥ (*uddīrṣvanārītyanayā mṛtaṃ patnyanurohati | bhrātā kanīyānpretasya nigadya pratiṣedhati ‖*) (13)
कुर्यादेतत्कर्म होता देवरो न भवेद्यदि । प्रेतानुगमनं न स्यादिति ब्राह्मणशासनात् ॥ (*kuryādetatkarma hotā devaro na bhavedyadi | pretānugamanaṃ na syāditi brāhmaṇaśāsanāt ‖*) (14)
वर्णानामितरेषां च स्त्रीधर्मोऽयं भवेन्न वा ॥ (*varṇānāmitareṣāṃ ca strīdharmo 'yaṃ bhavenna vā ‖*)
Reciting the Ṛk उदीर्घनारि (*udīrghanāri*), the wife of the dead man mounts the pyre, ready to go along with her husband. Then the husband's younger brother, her brother-in-law, prevents the woman from going along. If the dead man has no younger brother, the priest does that work. There is a Brāhmaṇa injunction that one should not go along with the corpse. For Brāhmaṇas and the other castes, as regards the wives of the dead, one may follow this rule if one wishes; otherwise one may leave it.
शांत्यर्थं धनुरादाने प्रेतस्यर्चं धनुर्जपेत् । यस्मादेताः प्रयुज्यंते श्मशाने चांत्यकर्मणि ॥ (*śāṃtyarthaṃ dhanurādāne pretasyarcaṃ dhanurjapet | yasmādetāḥ prayujyaṃte śmaśāne cāṃtyakarmaṇi ‖*) (15)
तस्माद्वदेत्तृचस्यास्य देवतां मृत्युमेव तु । (*tasmādvadettṛcasyāsya devatāṃ mṛtyumeva tu |*)
If the dead man was a Kṣatriya, for his peace, and when taking in hand the bow he used, to place it beside the body, this Ṛk धनुर्हस्तात् (*dhanurhastāt*) is to be recited. Since this Ṛk and the following ones are recited at the cremation ground in the final rites, Death is said to be the deity of these Ṛks.
मंत्रेषु ह्यनिरुक्तेषु देवतां कर्मतो वदेत्॥ (*maṃtreṣu hyanirukteṣu devatāṃ karmato vadet‖*) (16)
मंत्रतः कर्मतश्चैव प्रजापतिरसंभवे (*maṃtrataḥ karmataścaiva prajāpatirasaṃbhave*)
Where the mantras of this sūkta do not state their application or deity, the deity and application of each mantra should be stated according to the rite performed. Where nothing is clear, one may say that Prajāpati is the deity of those mantras, according to the meaning of the mantra and the rite performed.
पराश्चतस्रो यास्त्वत्र उप सर्पेति पार्थिवी॥ (*parāścatasro yāstvatra upa sarpeti pārthivī‖*) (17)
तासां प्रयोगः प्रेतस्य अस्थि संचयकर्मणि॥ (*tāsāṃ prayogaḥ pretasya asthi saṃcayakarmaṇi‖*)
The following four Ṛks, that is, the four Ṛks (10–13) beginning with the Ṛk उप सर्प (*upa sarpa*), are applied in the rite of asthisañcayana, part of the final rites (the gathering in one place of the bones of the dead body after cremation, to put them into a river and so on, is called asthisañcayana)

### Printed p. 579
and so on. (The rite is thus continued from the previous page.)
प्रतीचीने यथाहानि अपहृत्येतराणि तु ॥ (*pratīcīne yathāhāni apahṛtyetarāṇi tu ‖*) (18)
अहस्सु पितरो दधुरित्याशास्तेऽन्त्ययाशिषः । अहःस्वागामिषु च मां प्रयतं समजीवयन् ॥ (*ahassu pitaro dadhurityāśāste 'ntyayāśiṣaḥ | ahaḥsvāgāmiṣu ca māṃ prayataṃ samajīvayan ‖*) (19)
(Bṛ. De. 7-10 to 19)
In the last Ṛk, प्रतीचीने (*pratīcīne*), it is stated that the ancestral deities have given the blessing of increased life to the performer even on the days on which the rite is performed.
In the work called Ṛgvidhāna, attributed to Śaunaka, it is said of this sūkta:
मृत्युमेव प्रपद्येत परं मृत्यो जपन् द्विजः । नक्तभोजी मिताहारः परिसंवत्सरं सदा ॥ (*mṛtyumeva prapadyeta paraṃ mṛtyo japan dvijaḥ | naktabhojī mitāhāraḥ parisaṃvatsaraṃ sadā ‖*) (40)
नैनं पुरायुषो मृत्युर्नयते ससुतप्रजं (*nainaṃ purāyuṣo mṛtyurnayate sasutaprajaṃ*)
If a twice-born man mutters this sūkta परं मृत्यो (*paraṃ mṛtyo*), the deity Death becomes gracious and pleased with him. While muttering in this way he must fast by day and take a measured meal at night only. If he mutters thus for one year, the deity Death does not carry him, or his sons and other dependants, away before his appointed span of life is complete.
फलाहारो जयेन्मृत्युं त्रिभिर्वर्षैर्मिताशनः । षष्ठे काले तु भुंजीत फलं मूलमथापि वा ॥ (*phalāhāro jayenmṛtyuṃ tribhirvarṣairmitāśanaḥ | ṣaṣṭhe kāle tu bhuṃjīta phalaṃ mūlamathāpi vā ‖*)
Certain rules are to be followed while muttering with this deity Death in view. Every day he must fast by day, and in the sixth watch, that is, the second watch after sunset, eat only roots, fruits and the like. The man who mutters for three years with this scheme of measured food has no fear of death.
स्थानासनाभ्यां विहरेदुदके शिशिरे वसेश्॥ (*sthānāsanābhyāṃ viharedudake śiśire vaseś‖*) (42)
ग्रीष्मे पंचतपास्तु स्याद्वर्षास्वभ्रावकाशकः । एवं युक्तो जयेन्मृत्युं रोगेभ्यश्च प्रमुच्यते ॥ (*grīṣme paṃcatapāstu syādvarṣāsvabhrāvakāśakaḥ | evaṃ yukto jayenmṛtyuṃ rogebhyaśca pramucyate ‖*) (43)
While muttering, in the cold season (Śiśira) he must stand in the middle of water and mutter. In summer he must stand in the middle of the five fires and mutter. In the rainy season he must stand outside the house

### Printed p. 580
and mutter, getting wet in the rain. The man who mutters in this way removes the fear of death and lives free from disease.
भ्रातुर्भार्यामपुत्रस्य संतानार्थं मृते पत् । देवरोन्वारुरुक्षंतीमुदीर्ष्यति निवर्तयेत् ॥ (*bhrāturbhāryāmaputrasya saṃtānārthaṃ mṛte pat | devaronvārurukṣaṃtīmudīrṣyati nivartayet ‖*) (44)
ऋतुकाले तु संप्राप्ते घृताभ्यक्तोऽथ वाग्यतः । एकमुत्पादयेत्पुत्रं न द्वितीयं कथंचन ॥ (*ṛtukāle tu saṃprāpte ghṛtābhyakto 'tha vāgyataḥ | ekamutpādayetputraṃ na dvitīyaṃ kathaṃcana ‖*) (45)
(Ṛgvidhāna, chapter 3)
When an elder brother dies childless and his wife is ready to go along with the body on the pyre, the dead man's younger brother must prevent his elder brother's wife, his sister-in-law, from going along and bring her back home. Afterwards, when that woman has bathed after her period and been made pure with ghee-anointing and the like, he must have intercourse with her and beget one son only. He must never again, in any circumstances, be with that woman in order to have another son.
Concerning Death, the deity of this sūkta, there is a story in the Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa. In former times the gods and men performed sacrifices and the like and, as their fruit, went in their bodies to heaven and the other worlds. While this was so—
स मृत्युर्देवानब्रवीत् । अथैव सर्वे मनुष्या अमृता भविष्यंत्यथ को मह्यं भागो भविष्यतीति । ते होचुर्नातोः परः कश्चन सह शरीरेणामृतोऽसद्यदैव त्वमेतं भागं हरास्यॆ । अथ व्यावृत्य शरीरेणामृतोऽसद्विद्यया वा कर्मणा वेति । यद्वै तदब्रुवन् विद्यया वा कर्मणा वेति । एष हैव सा विद्या यदग्नि रेतदु हैव तत्कर्म यदग्निः । ते ये एवमेतद्विदुर्येवैतत्कर्म कुर्वते मृत्वा पुनस्संभवंति । ते ते संभवंत एव अमृतत्वमभिसंभवंति । अथ ये एवं न विदुर्ये वैतत्कर्म न कुर्वते मृत्वा पुनस्संभवंति ते एतस्यॆवान्नं पुनःपुनर्भवंति ॥ (*sa mṛtyurdevānabravīt | athaiva sarve manuṣyā amṛtā bhaviṣyaṃtyatha ko mahyaṃ bhāgo bhaviṣyatīti | te hocurnātoḥ paraḥ kaścana saha śarīreṇāmṛto 'sadyadaiva tvametaṃ bhāgaṃ harāsyè | atha vyāvṛtya śarīreṇāmṛto 'sadvidyayā vā karmaṇā veti | yadvai tadabruvan vidyayā vā karmaṇā veti | eṣa haiva sā vidyā yadagni retadu haiva tatkarma yadagniḥ | te ye evametadviduryevaitatkarma kurvate mṛtvā punassaṃbhavaṃti | te te saṃbhavaṃta eva amṛtatvamabhisaṃbhavaṃti | atha ye evaṃ na vidurye vaitatkarma na kurvate mṛtvā punassaṃbhavaṃti te etasyèvānnaṃ punaḥpunarbhavaṃti ‖*)
(Śa. Brā. 10-4-3-9, 10)
Once upon a time Death spoke to the gods thus: "O gods, by performing good works such as sacrifice you have gained freedom from death (immortality: living always without dying). In the same way all men, performing sacrifices and the like, will gain immortality (eternal happiness in heaven). Then what is my work? What am I to do? No one dies at all!"

### Printed p. 581
(This window continues the Special Topics begun on the previous page.)

When Death had said this, the gods replied: "Very well. From now on, even though human beings perform good deeds and become fit for immortality or the bliss of heaven, let them not go to heaven with their bodies. Take possession of their bodies. Then, falling under the power of Death, they will leave their breath and their bodies here and go to heaven with a different body." Therefore from that time onward, human beings who have become fit for immortality, whether through knowledge or through good works, attain immortality (the eternal bliss of heaven) only after they have abandoned the body here and died. Here "by knowledge or by work" means knowledge or work relating to Agni. Those who know this and perform the work attain immortality after death. Those who do not know it, however much work they do, are born again and again after death and fall under the power of death in every birth. So it is said.

A remarkable situation is described in the Aitareya Brāhmaṇa:

स वा एष न कदाचनास्तमेति नोदेति । तं यदस्तमेतीति मन्यंतेऽह्य एव तदंतमित्वाथात्मानं विपर्यस्यते रात्रीमेवास्तात्कुरुशेऽहः परस्तात् । अथ यदेनं प्रातरुदेतीति मन्यंते रात्रेरेव तदंतमित्वाथात्मानं विपर्यस्यतेऽहरेवावस्तात्कुरुते रात्रिं परस्तात् । स वा एष न कदाचन निमोचति ! न ह वै कदाचन निम्मोचत्येतस्य ह सायुज्यं सरूपतां सलोकतामश्नुतेय एवं वेद (*sa vā eṣa na kadācanāstameti nodeti | taṃ yadastametīti manyaṃte 'hya eva tadaṃtamitvāthātmānaṃ viparyasyate rātrīmevāstātkuruśe 'haḥ parastāt | atha yadenaṃ prātarudetīti manyaṃte rātrereva tadaṃtamitvāthātmānaṃ viparyasyate 'harevāvastātkurute rātriṃ parastāt | sa vā eṣa na kadācana nimocati ! na ha vai kadācana nimmocatyetasya ha sāyujyaṃ sarūpatāṃ salokatāmaśnuteya evaṃ veda*)
(Ai. Brā. 14-44)

In ordinary usage we say that the sun rises and sets. In truth the sun stays where he is; he neither rises nor sets. When people think that the sun sets, in reality he does not set. At the end of the day, the regions on the two sides of the sun have night and day at the same moment: when it is day on the side facing the sun, it is night on the other side. Likewise, when it is said that the sun rises in the morning, that too is not the real state of affairs. At the time when one side of the sun is dark, that is, in night, day is dawning on the other side. Even then, on the two sides of the sun, night on one side and day on the other are seen at the same moment. Moreover, where there was night before there is now day, and where there was day there is now night. This is seen as a succession of changes; the sun never sets, that is, never sinks. When we think he has set, he is making day in another region and shining there. 

### Printed p. 582
The man who knows this course of the sun reaches the world of the sun and attains union with the sun (sāyujya). That is, having obtained a luminous divine body, he becomes inwardly part of the Lord in the form of the sun and attains immortality. For him there is no old age, death, rebirth or sorrow; he is always immersed in eternal bliss. Thus the excellent state of life after death is described.

On the course attained after death, the conversation and the inquiry into the truth between Naciketas, the son of a sage of the Gautama gotra, and the deity Death are given briefly in the 8th anuvāka of Taittirīya Brāhmaṇa 3-11. The same is described at length and critically in the Kaṭha Upaniṣad. Since the whole of that Upaniṣad consists of their dialogue, only its substance is given here.

**A brief account of the Kaṭhopaniṣad**

Long ago there was a sage. He had a son named Naciketas, still a boy. At that time the sage set about performing the sacrifice called Viśvajit. The rule of that sacrifice is that the sacrificer must give all his possessions to Brāhmaṇas. The sage was poor and had nothing of value to give. So he gave away some old, emaciated, lame cows that were no longer able to give the milk they had left. The sage's son, the boy Naciketas, watching all this, thought in his mind: "My father has performed this excellent sacrifice for the attainment of the best worlds and has given gifts as the scriptures prescribe. But when one gives, one should give good things. The things given should be a means of happiness for those who receive them and should be useful to them. Only by giving useful things does one gain well-being. But what benefit have the Brāhmaṇas received from these emaciated, old cows, unable to give milk, which my father has given? Merit cannot come from a gift of this kind." Thinking thus, he said to his father: "Father, in this sacrifice you have not given away everything you have. For the fruit of the sacrifice to be obtained in full, you must give away everything in your possession. There is still one thing of yours that you have not given away. What is it? It is I, who belong to you and am your son. To whom will you give me?" The father took this for a child's talk and did not trouble to answer. Naciketas asked the same question again; even then the father said nothing. When Naciketas pressed the same question a third time, the father grew angry, and in the heat of his anger said: "I give you to Death (to Yama, the deity of death)." Thereupon, satisfied, Naciketas resolved to carry out his father's word and made ready to go to Death.

### Printed p. 583
But the father repented of what he had said in anger and tried with soothing words to turn his son from his resolve; Naciketas did not wish to break his father's word. Then a bodiless voice was heard: "Boy, go to the house of Death; find out the time when he is at home. Your wish will be fulfilled." Encouraged by those words, Naciketas went to the house of Death. But Death was not at home. It was three days before he came home. For those three days Naciketas stayed there fasting and waited for Death to come. When Death came and saw the young celibate student Naciketas, who had been fasting for three days in his house waiting for him, he said in repentance: "Boy, homage to you. I have learned that you have fasted for three days in my house. When a guest fasts, there is no well-being. Therefore, for the three days you fasted, ask for three boons of your choice; I will grant them." The boy asked for a boon thus: "Let my father's anger be quieted. When I return from you, let my father recognise me and receive me lovingly. Let my father's anxiety be gone and his mind be at peace. This is the first boon I ask." Yama (Death) granted it, saying "So be it," and said: "Ask for your second boon."

Then Naciketas asked that the method of worshipping Agni, the means to heaven, and the knowledge of it be granted to him. Yama, pleased with his keen intelligence, gave the boon accordingly, and also granted the boon that this Agni, fit for sacrifice, should be famous by his name (नाचिकेतमग्निं (*nāciketamagniṃ*)).

Then Naciketas asked about his third boon: "Some say that when a man has died his self exists, others say that it does not. You alone are able to give certain knowledge on this matter. I wish to learn the certain knowledge about it from you. Tell it to me clearly. This is the third boon I ask." Hearing this,

Yama: Boy, even the gods in former times debated this matter at length. It cannot be understood easily; it is a most subtle matter. Naciketas, do not insist, do not press me; ask another boon and I will give it.

Naciketas: You yourself have said that even the gods did not understand what I ask and that they debated it much. Apart from you, nobody else knows this matter.

### Printed p. 584
You alone are able to explain it. There is no boon better than this. Please grant it to me.

Yama: Boy, ask for sons and grandsons who will live a hundred years; ask for elephants and horses, cattle and other livestock, gold, and wide fields. I will give you as many years of life as you wish. I will give you whatever you wish. Ask for every kind of wealth. Ask for whatever desired things are unobtainable on earth. I will give chariots, charming beautiful women, and all desired things. But do not ask the question about death.

Naciketas: Yama, all the things you wish to give are momentary and perishable. Why more? Our very life lasts only a short time. After death, what use are the things you give, the chariots and the rest? All will become yours again. However much wealth there is, man is not satisfied by it. As long as you favour me, there is no difficulty for my life. Having come to the world of the gods, who are free from old age and death, can a mortal ask for fleeting pleasures? God of Death, I want no other boon except this one: the truth about which so much has been debated, which is of great importance in the other world, and which is hidden.

Yama: Boy, since you have asked so much, I will tell you; listen. In the world there are two paths, the better (śreyas) and the pleasanter (preyas). These two are different, and their results are different. The man moved by the pleasanter (that is, worldly pleasures) engages in action, and his human goal is lost. But the man who follows the path of the better attains all good. Therefore the wise man, knowing that of the two the better is the more excellent, seeks the better. The fool, captivated by worldly things, desires the pleasanter. Naciketas, you have, after consideration, given up many dear things and the pleasures of this world. Though many people desire the path of the pleasanter, rich in wealth and grain, you did not desire it. In the world ignorance and knowledge are wholly different. You are one who desires knowledge, for you were not deluded by desires, by sense pleasures, or by the pleasures and joys of this world. Those enveloped in ignorance, thinking themselves very wise, are led astray like one blind man following another. The man who is foolish like a child, captivated by wealth and the like, has no discrimination between fit and unfit. He thinks that there is only this visible world and no other world beyond. 

### Printed p. 585
As a result he is born again and again and in each birth falls under my power (the power of Death). Many do not get the opportunity to hear and understand that knowledge which is the highest, the knowledge of the Self (knowledge of Brahman). A teacher who can teach such knowledge is also hard to find. Even when a teacher is found, that interest should arise and a desire to understand the knowledge of the Self should be born is truly a wonder. Because there are many kinds of differing opinions about the knowledge of the Self, if an ordinary man speaks of it, it is not well understood. Only a knower of the Self of proper qualification should teach it. For a pupil taught by such a teacher there is nothing left unknown; he knows everything and becomes all-knowing. This knowledge of the Self cannot be understood by mere reasoning or conjecture; it must be understood from a wise teacher. Naciketas, there is no other like you, a seeker of truth, who asks about the knowledge of the Self with the eagerness to understand it. Riches and the like are impermanent; by the help of impermanent things the knowledge of Brahman, which is permanent, cannot be attained. Naciketas, you have despised other worldly riches and desired only the highest state, which grants all desires, is the abode of perfect happiness and is exceedingly vast, and have given up other pleasures. The discerning man, realising by the knowledge gained through yoga the Self, which is hard to see, set in the hidden cave of the heart, eternal and shining with brilliance, crosses over joy and sorrow. The man who has heard and understood this realises the Self and enjoys bliss, thinking that the very abode of bliss has been gained by him. I know that the door of such an abode of bliss stands open for you, Naciketas.

Naciketas: Tell me clearly that which you know to be different from dharma and adharma, different from cause and effect, and different from past and future.

Yama: I will tell you briefly of the highest goal which all the Vedas praise, for the attainment of which the discerning observe celibacy and perform hard austerity. It is the syllable Om, the praṇava. This is the imperishable Brahman. This is the imperishable, that is, the indestructible. One who has gained knowledge of this syllable obtains whatever highest state he desires. This is the best of all means. One who knows this means is honoured even in the world of Brahmā. The Self, whose nature is knowledge, has no birth or death. That Self is not produced from another thing; it was never produced. It is unborn (without origin), permanent, eternal, ancient. Therefore even when the body dies, the Self dwelling in the body is not destroyed. 

### Printed p. 586
Those who say "I will kill" or "I shall be killed" are nothing but ignorant, for the Self neither kills nor is killed. The Self in the cave of the heart of living beings is smaller than the smallest, that is, exceedingly subtle; since it pervades everywhere, it is greater than the greatest. Only one free from desire has sight of the Self. One free from sorrow understands the greatness of the Self through the grace of the Supreme Self. Though seated in one place, the Self can go far; though lying down, it can move everywhere. Who but I can know the Self, endowed with such qualities, joyful and free from sorrow? The discerning man who has realised this all-pervading and supreme Self, which is bodiless though in bodies (that is, takes no part in the pleasures and pains that belong to the body) and permanent among the impermanent, becomes free from sorrow; that is, for him there is no sorrow at all. This knowledge of the Self is not obtained by exposition (by reading and studying the scriptures and the like), nor by intellect, nor by hearing what others say. Only the man who desires to realise the Self, to whom the Self shows favour, that is, with whom the Self is pleased, can obtain this Self; the Self reveals its own true nature to him. The man who has not abandoned evil deeds, who is restless, whose mind is not concentrated, in whose mind peace does not dwell, cannot realise the Self, however much knowledge he has. Brāhmaṇas, Kṣatriyas and all classes of people, and even Death, are the food of the Self (that is, subject to it): can one easily know where such a Self is?

Yama continued his explanation: Dwelling in the cave of the man's inmost heart, enjoying the fruits of action, the two selves, the individual self and the Supreme Self, are always, say the knowers of Brahman, like shade and sunlight, that is, like light and its shadow, one always beside the other. We know the Agni called Naciketas, a bridge that carries over the ocean of worldly existence the devoted who perform sacrifices and other rites and worship Brahman, and also the Supreme Brahman, who gives fearlessness to those who wish to cross the ocean of worldly existence and carries them across. This body is a chariot. The Self is the lord of the chariot seated in it. The intellect is the charioteer. The mind is the bridle that holds the horses in control; the senses are the horses. The pleasures of sense objects, which belong to the senses, are the road. The discerning say that the Self joined to the senses and mind is the one who experiences pleasure and pain. Since the mind is always of restless nature, the senses of one without pure knowledge, like bad horses that do not obey the charioteer, are self-willed and do not remain under his control. That is, just as bad horses are not under the control of the charioteer, so too, of one without pure knowledge

### Printed p. 587
(The sentence from the preceding page continues.) The senses (the mind, eyes, ears and the rest) are not under his control. But for a man who has knowledge, the senses remain under his control, as well-trained horses stay under their charioteer's. The man who lacks knowledge, whose mind is unsteady and who is always impure, does not attain the highest state. For him the entanglement of saṃsāra, consisting of birth and death, remains: he is born, dies, and is born again in another birth. But only the man who has knowledge, a steady mind and purity attains the highest state (liberation). He does not come back from that highest state, and for him there is no further birth or death. The man who makes knowledge his charioteer and keeps his mind under restraint crosses the ocean of saṃsāra and reaches the all-pervading highest state. That supreme place (liberation) is said to be the highest abode of Viṣṇu.

Beyond the senses, that is, subtler than the senses, are the objects, or the tanmātras, which are the subtle forms of the five elements (tanmātra means subtle form). Beyond the tanmātras of the five elements is the mind; beyond the mind is the intellect; beyond that the great self; beyond that the supreme Unmanifest; beyond that the Puruṣa (Parabrahma), who is higher still. Nothing is higher than this Puruṣa. That is the last, the supreme goal (gati).

This supreme Puruṣa is the Self hidden in the bodies of all beings, that is, of living creatures. He cannot be seen with the outer eye; nobody can see him. But he becomes visible to the subtle intellect of yogis and ascetics. That is, he is visible only to the inward-turned, keen intellect of ascetics who can directly perceive the subtlest things. The man of intellect should merge his speech into the mind, which is subtler than it. Then he should merge the mind into the Self made of knowledge or consciousness, which is subtler still. Then he should merge that conscious Self into the great Self, and the great Self into the peaceful Self. Therefore, people, arise! Rise up and be ready to act. Go to knowers who are greater than you and hear and learn the knowledge of Brahman. The effort to learn this knowledge of Brahman is as hard as walking on the edge of a sharp sword; the poets who know the truth say that this path is just as hard to traverse. This Self is soundless, touchless, imperishable and formless; that is, it cannot be known by hearing a sound, cannot be touched, and cannot be seen with the eye. It is always without destruction. And it is tasteless, that is, it cannot be known by the mouth, by the tongue; and as it has no smell, its nature cannot be known by smelling it. It is without beginning, and without end

### Printed p. 588
that is, it has no limit of place or time. Because it always exists it is beginningless; because it pervades everywhere it is endless. He who knows the Self-principle, whose nature is truth, which is beyond the great principle (mahat), that is, subtler than it and the cause of its origin, is freed from the mouth of death; that is, he has no fear of death, said Yama. The one who recites, and the one who hears, this narrative told by the god of death, Yama, to Naciketas is honoured and revered in the world of Brahmā. And the man who recites this supremely secret narrative to others, whether in an assembly of Brahmins or at a śrāddha, finds that the rite he performs yields endless fruit.

Continuing his conversation with Naciketas, Yama, the god of death, said further:

Yama: The self-existent Supreme Self let his powers flow outward. Therefore the senses can see only outer things; the inner Self, of the subtlest form, is not within their range. If a discerning man desires immortality (freedom from death, that is, the state of liberation), he turns inward (only through austerity and meditation) and sees the inner Self directly. Dull-witted people, like children, run after outer pleasures and fall into the wide net of death; that is, unable to gain liberation, they are caught in the ocean of saṃsāra, consisting of birth and death, and grieve. But the wise (those who seek knowledge of the Self), knowing the bliss of the immortal state, do not long for the impermanent things of this world. They do not think that the permanent can be obtained by gaining these impermanent things. The knowledge of the pleasure that arises from the five kinds of sense-pleasure (form, taste, smell, sound and touch) and from sexual union comes only from this Self. That by which this knowledge of pleasure arises is the Self. What else remains? Only the Self. Having directly known the great, all-pervading Self, by whose power the activities of the dream state and the waking state are known, the wise man gives no room to any grief. For him there is no sorrow or suffering. He who knows the Self, which is close to the bodily life, which enjoys the fruit of action and which is lord of past and future, becomes fearless; he is free of every fear and anxiety and lives without care. That which existed before austerity, that is, from beginningless time, which existed before the creation of water and the other principles, which entered the cave of the heart (unseen by anyone) and, in connection with the five elements (that is, in connection with the various parts of the body), is perceived by the wise: this is the Self. Aditi, the goddess who embodies all the gods, arose from it (from this Self); it dwells hidden in the bodies of living creatures in connection with the five elements: this is the Self. And just as in the womb of women

### Printed p. 589
the child is hidden, so Agni dwells hidden between the two araṇis (fire-sticks); he carries the oblations offered by the sacrificers in sacrifices to the gods, and is worshipped with great care each day. This Agni is the Self. From the Self the sun rises (is born). The setting of the sun is also in the Self. All the gods are born in the Self and are dissolved there. Such all-powerful capacity belongs to the Self. As it is here, so it is there; as it is there, so it is here. He who sees diversity in the Self, who is deluded by the ignorance that "I am one thing and the Self another", falls again and again into birth and death. To think that there is diversity is merely a delusion of the mind. There is no diversity here (in the Self). He who imagines diversity comes again and again to death. It is necessary to explain here what diversity means. In the world there are many and varied masses of living beings. In all of them the one Self dwells as the inner self, hidden in the heart. So he who attributes diversity, thinking that these masses of beings and the Self in them are different, that the Self in this creature is one thing and the Self in another creature another, is subject to death again and again. Though there are many living beings, the Self dwelling in all of them is one, not different. That it dwells at one time in the bodies of many creatures is the Self's distinctive feature and his greatness. To think, without knowing this, that the Self in the bodies of the various creatures is different is folly. The Self dwelling in a man's inner organ, that is, in the middle of the heart, is called the Puruṣa. This Puruṣa is of the measure of a thumb (aṅguṣṭha). That is, though the Self is all-pervading and pervades the whole universe, in the heart of creatures he is only of the small size of a thumb. Even so, this Puruṣa (the Self) is lord and controller of past and future. He who knows this becomes fearless. This Puruṣa of the measure of a thumb shines clearly like a smokeless fire. He is lord of past and future. He who exists today is he, and he who exists tomorrow is he. He is eternal.

Rain falling on mountain peaks flows in the surrounding regions as separate streams. The unwise man, not knowing that the separate streams fell from one rain, thinks the streams are different; so he thinks that the various bodies of creatures and the Self in them are different. Therefore he takes various births in various creatures. Hence one should not suppose that there is difference in the Self. O Gautama (Naṭakeśa, born in the Gotama line), when pure water is mixed with pure water, the two become one and uniform, without any difference; likewise the self of the knower of Brahman merges and becomes one in the Self of the same form, that is, the Self whose form is Brahman. That is, the knower of Brahman becomes lord in the Self (Brahman).

### Printed p. 590
Yama: Yama said further: This body is called a city. It has eleven gates: the head (brahmarandhra), the navel, two eyes, two ears, two nostrils, the mouth, and the two lower openings, that is, the passages for water and waste; eleven gates in all. In such a city, the body, dwells the pure conscious Self, free of birth and destruction. He who meditates on such a Self becomes free of sorrow. Liberated while living, after death he attains the liberation called the highest state. There is a mantra called the Haṃsavatī Ṛk, famous by its opening हंसः शुचिषत् (*haṃsaḥ śuciṣat*). Although the sun is the deity of this mantra, its meaning is explained here by saying that the Self which illumines the world in the form of Āditya is the sun. This Self (the Self existing in the form of Āditya) dwells in the sky as the sun, in the atmosphere as wind, on the sacrificial altar as fire, and in the sacrificer's house as a venerable guest. That is, that Self pervades men and the best among them, truth, and the sky. Water-born creatures, plants and the like growing on earth, the class of animals, the acts that are parts of sacrifice, rivers and the like arising on mountains and so on, and whatever other things there are in the world, all of these are this Self; that is, they are of the nature of the Self (a part of the Self). It is of the nature of truth and very extensive. It raises the prāṇa breath in the body upward and presses the apāna breath downward. All the gods worship this Self, seated in the middle of the body, as venerable. When the embodied being (the creature) departs from the body (that is, dies), what remains here after it has left this body? Nothing. That is, when a man dies and leaves the dead body, the Self does not dwell in that dead body. Men do not live by the power of the prāṇa breath nor by the strength of the apāna breath. People live by the strength of the Self, on whom these two depend. That is, it is said that a man lives only as long as the Self is in the body. After the Self has left the body, there are in that dead body neither the prāṇa and apāna breaths nor consciousness; only the inert body remains.

O Gautama, I shall tell you this secret of the eternal Brahman; listen. I shall also tell you in what state the Self is after death; listen. The discerning man, by gaining knowledge of Brahman, is freed from this saṃsāra and after death reaches the highest, supreme state. From there onward he has no rebirths or deaths. He remains happy, united with the always eternal and blissful Parabrahma. But the fool without knowledge of Brahman, after death, goes on to be born again and die again, wandering in the ocean of saṃsāra. Living beings such as men, according to their own actions and their own knowledge

### Printed p. 591
that is, as the fruit of the good and evil deeds they did in this life, are born in various wombs, that is, bodies, such as those of animals. Some take on an inert form. Even when creatures are asleep, the Self within their bodies is always awake and fashions forms (desires and aspirations) in keeping with their wishes. This is the pure, clean, eternal Brahman. All worlds rest on this Self (or Brahman). No one can go beyond it; that is, apart from Brahman there is no other thing. But then, in the world some creatures are big and some small, and the body of each creature is of a different kind. Is the Self in all these also of many kinds? If so, has not diversity and difference been ascribed to the Self? No, not so. The Self in the bodies of all creatures is one. According to circumstance and according to the bodies of the creatures, it dwells in bodies small and large and of many kinds, and is the witness of the deeds and so on done by those creatures. As fire that has entered a house takes on forms matching the things in it (when the fire is kindled), so the one Self within all beings takes on many forms and pervades things inside and outside. Likewise, as one and the same wind, entering many things, takes on forms matching those things, so the one Self, the inner self of all beings, takes on many forms and pervades the inside and outside of all things. And when sea water is filled into various vessels, that water takes on various forms according to the shape and form of each vessel. In the same way the one Self pervades, inside and outside, the bodies of the various creatures according to their shapes and forms. Does then the Self in creatures not have pleasure and pain? No. Pleasure, pain and the like belong only to the body and other parts of creatures. The Self, which is in them in the form of consciousness, has none of them; he is unattached. How? The sun, the eye of all the worlds, shines casting his rays everywhere upon all things, yet he has no contact with those things, that is, with their pleasures and pains; in the same way the one Self dwelling in all beings has no contact with the pleasure and pain of those beings or creatures. He is unattached to the suffering of the world. He is outside the world. Those wise ones who see in the Self in the middle of their own body that Self (the Supreme Self), the inner self of all beings, lord of all, who manifests one form as many forms, that is, who know that the Supreme Self, indwelling in all, and the Self dwelling in their own body in the form of consciousness are one, obtain imperishable happiness. Others do not obtain that happiness. All other things are impermanent, that is, not lasting; they exist for some time and are destroyed. But the Self is not so; he is eternal. For him always

### Printed p. 592
there is no destruction. Therefore those wise ones who know that the Supreme Self, the eternal among the impermanent, the one conscious being among all conscious beings, the fulfiller of the desires, that is, the aspirations, of all people, is in their own self, enjoy imperishable, eternal happiness. Others do not have that eternal happiness. People take this to be the indescribable (that is, inexpressible) supreme happiness. How am I to know it? Who knows whether it comes within experience or not? That is: in that supreme place called the highest state (liberation, or the unchanging Self) the sun does not shine as he does in this world. There is no light of moon and stars there, nor the light of lightning. What then of fire? There is no fire there. Then is that highest state always covered in deep darkness? No, not so. That Self is by nature self-luminous. Not only that: once it shines, everything shines by its light. By its light everything is lit.

The description of the highest state is given in another way: this is saṃsāra, the stream of birth and death, which is the eternal aśvattha tree (is like an aśvattha tree). Its roots are above, that is, spread upward; its branches are below, that is, grown downward. The root of that tree (what is its cause) is the pure thing, Brahman. That is, the meaning is that this saṃsāra and the outer world have come into being from Brahman, the pure thing. This pure Brahman is called immortal (amṛta means without destruction). All worlds rest on it. No one can go beyond it. Only if there were a thing other than this Brahman would the question of going beyond it arise. Since it is the final place, there is nothing further, nothing beyond it. This whole universe visible to us moves in prāṇa, that is, in Brahman, who is the form of consciousness in prāṇa and all-pervading. That is, the origin and dissolution of this universe take place in Brahman. This Brahman, the cause of the universe, is very great, that is, without beginning or end, endless. When one goes on reflecting on this infinite nature, one feels: how great it is! How small is this universe and the creatures in it! This feeling arises and causes a kind of fear in the mind. As fearful as it is to see a man lift a thunderbolt in his hand, ready to strike, so fearful is it to contemplate the stature of this infinite Brahman. It does not come within the reach of man's intellect, because man's intellect has a limit. Yet ascetics and knowers who have realised the Self through yoga and other practices know this and become immortal. Through fear (that is, by the command) of this Supreme Self or Brahman, the cause of the origin, continuance and dissolution of the universe, fire burns, that is, fire has the power to burn; the sun

### Printed p. 593

…the Brahman—through fear of it the sun shines, and Indra, Vāyu and Yama (or Mṛtyu), the fifth, perform their respective duties through fear of him (Brahman).

It is good if self-knowledge comes before this body falls (dies). Otherwise the soul must take birth in the various worlds of creation. As one's reflection is seen in a mirror, so Brahman is seen clearly in one's own self. That is, to one who knows the Self, the realisation of Brahman appears as clearly as a face in a mirror. In the world of the Fathers it appears indistinctly, as in a dream. In the world of the Gandharvas it appears indistinctly, as a reflection in water. But in the world of Brahman the vision of Brahman is clear, as light (sunshine) and shade are clearly seen.

The wise man who understands the differing states of the senses, born from the different tanmātras, and their origin and dissolution, becomes free from sorrow. That is, the senses such as the eye, born from the tanmātras (tanmātra means subtle form) of the five elements beginning with earth, are in the end dissolved or destroyed in the five elements, their place of origin. These five elements and the senses born of them last for some time and perish. But the wise man who knows that the Self is never destroyed has no sorrow at all.

The mind is higher, or subtler, than the senses. Pure intellect is greater than the mind. Higher and subtler than the intellect is the Mahat principle. Beyond it, that is subtler than it, is the Unmanifest. Higher than the Unmanifest is Puruṣa (cit, or consciousness). This is the Self. He is all-pervading, without any characteristic marks, free from all the attributes of worldly existence, unattached. Knowing such a Self, a living being becomes free and attains immortality. The form of this Self does not come within sight (outer sight). No one can see him with the eye. He becomes visible only through meditation in the inner organ of a yogī or ascetic with controlled mind. Those who know this also become immortal.

For the one whose five organs of knowledge and mind are steady and whose intellect is unmoving, that is, who has gained firmness of mind without letting his mental modifications go towards the pleasures of the senses, they say the supreme state has been reached. This steady holding of the senses is called yoga. The yogī must be very vigilant, for even the state of yoga has many pitfalls or obstacles. For one who is not vigilant, that is, who is slothful, yoga is not accomplished. Self-knowledge is not obtained by speech (conversation and the like), by thinking with the mind, or by seeing with the eyes.

### Printed p. 594

It is attained only by one who has firm faith that it (the Self) exists, that is, one of believing mind, a man of faith. It must be obtained through true knowledge of cause and effect. When the conviction that it exists is born, true knowledge (knowledge of Brahman) becomes manifest, that is, arises in the mind. When all the desires in a man's inner organ, that is, the longing for pleasures and the like, are destroyed, he becomes immortal, that is, liberated while living, and enjoys the bliss of Brahman here itself. When the false bonds that have made a home in the inner organ (the mind) are destroyed, the mortal man becomes immortal, that is, he attains the eternal supreme state called liberation. As soon as the bonds of ignorance firmly lodged in a man's heart are destroyed, the mortal becomes immortal. In the heart there are one hundred and one channels (nāḍīs). Among them one channel called Suṣumnā goes up to the Brahma-randhra at the top of the head. If the breath is made to move in that channel and the life-breath departs through the Brahma-randhra, that man attains immortality. If the breath departs through the other channels, he obtains various births hereafter.

The Puruṣa of the size of a thumb, that is, the inner Self, always dwells in people's hearts. To see that inner Self one must separate it with patience, that is, with self-knowledge, as one peels off a husk and takes out the thing within. That is the immortal thing shining with divine radiance.

Having understood this knowledge of Brahman taught by Mṛtyu or Yama, and having learned the whole method of yoga which he taught, Naciketas attained the state of Brahman. He became free from sin and immortal. Other people too who understand the knowledge of the Self set forth in it will attain eternal liberation like Naciketas.

Here ends the concise exposition of the Kaṭha Upaniṣad.

### Printed p. 595

##### ॥ सायणभाष्यम् ॥ (Sāyaṇa-bhāṣya)

> परं मृत्यो इति चतुर्दशर्च० द्वितीयं सूक्तं । यमपुत्रस्य संकुसुकस्यार्ष० । एकादशी प्रस्तारपंक्तिः । आद्या जागतौ ततो द्वा गायत्रौ । प्रस्तारपंक्तिः
> पुरतः । पि ३-४० । इति । त्रयोदशी जगती चतुर्दर्श्यनुष्टुप् । शिष्टास्त्रिष्टुभः ।
> तत्रादौ चतस्रो मृत्युदेवत्याः । पंचमी धातृदेवताका । षष्ठि त्वष्टृदेवत्या ।
> सप्तम्याद्याः शिष्टाः पितृमेधाभिधायिन्यः । अतस्तद्देवताकाः । अंत्या त्वनिरुक्तत्वा-

##### Gist of the bhāṣya

The sūkta "परं मृत्यो (*paraṃ mṛtyo*)" (a fourteen-Ṛk sūkta, the second) has as its seer Saṅkusuka, son of Yama. The eleventh verse is a prastāra-paṅkti; the first is a jagatī and then two are gāyatrī; the prastāra-paṅkti is said to come first (a reference is cited, printed पि ३-४० (*pi 3-40*)). The thirteenth is jagatī, the fourteenth anuṣṭubh, and the rest triṣṭubh. Of these, the first four have Mṛtyu as deity, the fifth Dhātṛ, the sixth Tvaṣṭṛ. The seventh and the rest are about the Pitṛmedha (funeral rite); hence they have the Fathers and the like as deities. The last is either Prājāpatya, because no deity is stated for it.**NOTE**

> त्प्राजापत्या वा । तथा चानुक्रांतं । परं मृत्यो संकुसुकश्चतस्रो मृत्युदेवताः
> परा धात्रि परा त्वाष्ट्री पराः पितृमेधा एकादशी प्रस्तारपंक्तिर्जगत्युपांत्यांत्यानुष्टुप् प्राजापत्या वा सानिरुक्तेति ॥

##### Gist of the bhāṣya

So also the Anukramaṇī says: परं मृत्यो संकुसुकश्चतस्रो मृत्युदेवताः परा धात्रि परा त्वाष्ट्री पराः पितृमेधा एकादशी प्रस्तारपंक्तिर्जगत्युपांत्यांत्यानुष्टुप् प्राजापत्या वा सानिरुक्तेति ॥ (*paraṃ mṛtyo saṃkusukaścatasro mṛtyudevatāḥ parā dhātri parā tvāṣṭrī parāḥ pitṛmedhā ekādaśī prastārapaṃktirjagatyupāṃtyāṃtyānuṣṭup prājāpatyā vā sānirukteti ‖*)

##### Anuvāda

This sūkta "परं मृत्यो (*paraṃ mṛtyo*)" is the second sūkta in the second anuvāka. It has fourteen Ṛks. Its seer is Saṅkusuka, son of Yama. Its eleventh Ṛk is in the prastāra-paṅkti metre; the first two Ṛks are in jagatī; the next two (Ṛks 3–4) in gāyatrī; the thirteenth Ṛk in jagatī; the fourteenth in anuṣṭubh; the remaining Ṛks in triṣṭubh. The first four Ṛks of this sūkta have Mṛtyu as deity; the fifth has Dhātṛ; the sixth has Tvaṣṭṛ; from the seventh onward all Ṛks are used in the subsequent rite called Pitṛmedhābhidhāyinī, so for them the Fathers and others are the deities. As no deity is specified for the last Ṛk, Prajāpati may be its deity. The Anukramaṇī says: Parā mṛtyo ….

Sūkta 18
Maṇḍala 10 · Anuvāka 2 · Sūkta 18
Aṣṭaka 7 · Adhyāya 6 · Vargas 26, 27, 28
Number of Ṛks in the sūkta: 14
Seer: Saṅkusuka Yāmāyana.
Deity: 1–4 Mṛtyu; 5 Dhātṛ; 6 Tvaṣṭṛ; 7–13 Pitṛmedha; 14 Pitṛmedha or Prajāpati.
Metre: 1–10, 12 triṣṭubh; 11 prastāra-paṅkti; 13 jagatī; 14 anuṣṭubh.

#### Ṛk 1

##### ॥ संहितापाठः ॥ (Saṃhitā-pāṭha)

> परं॑ मृत्यो॒ अनु॒ परे॑हि॒ पंथां॒ यस्ते॒ स्व इत॑रो देव॒याना॑त् ।  
> चक्षु॑ष्मते शृण्व॒ते ते॑ ब्रवीमि॒ मा नः॑ प्र॒जां री॑रिषो॒ मोत  ॒
> वीरान् ॥ १ ॥

### Printed p. 596
